verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar sets up an image of gold ninety feet high on the plain of Dura and summons all his officials to its dedication (vv. 1-3). A herald proclaims that when the music sounds all must fall down and worship the golden image, or be thrown into a burning fiery furnace (vv. 4-6). At the sound of the music, all the peoples bow (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Every earthly power that demands the worship belonging to God must be refused.

verseByVerse.quote: King Nebuchadnezzar made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits and its breadth six cubits. He set it up on the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent to gather the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the justices, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces to come to the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. Then the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the justices, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces gathered for the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. And they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Nebuchadnezzar made an image of gold, whose height was sixty cubits and its breadth six cubits. He set it up on the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.

The ESV notes that a cubit was about eighteen inches, so this image stood some ninety feet tall and nine feet wide. It may have been a statue on a high base, or a tall pillar with a figure on it. Either way, it towered over the flat plain and could be seen for miles. It was probably covered with gold rather than solid gold, but it would have blazed in the sun.

The text does not tell us what the image represented. It may have been one of Babylon's gods, or the king himself, or both at once, since in the ancient world loyalty to the king and loyalty to his gods went together. Many readers have also noticed the link with chapter 2. There God showed Nebuchadnezzar that he was only a head of gold, and that his kingdom would pass away. Here he builds an image that is gold from top to bottom. Whether or not he meant it this way, it looks like a king answering God's message with his own: my kingdom will last.

Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent to gather the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the justices, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces to come to the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

Then the satraps, the prefects, and the governors, the counselors, the treasurers, the justices, the magistrates, and all the officials of the provinces gathered for the dedication of the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up. And they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

The writer gives the long list of officials twice, and the phrase the image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up again and again. The effect is deliberate, and a little humorous. We see the whole machinery of the state, every rank of government official, lined up in rows before a statue. The repeated phrase keeps reminding us where this god came from. It did not come from heaven. A man set it up.

That is always the truth about idols. Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands (Ps 115:4). And the psalm adds a warning: Those who make them become like them (Ps 115:8). The officials on the plain of Dura stood as still and silent as the statue they served.

verseByVerse.quote: And the herald proclaimed aloud, "You are commanded, O peoples, nations, and languages, that when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, you are to fall down and worship the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up. And whoever does not fall down and worship shall immediately be cast into a burning fiery furnace." Therefore, as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, all the peoples, nations, and languages fell down and worshiped the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the herald proclaimed aloud, "You are commanded, O peoples, nations, and languages,

that when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, you are to fall down and worship the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar has set up.

This was not only a religious ceremony. It was a test of loyalty for an empire made up of many peoples, nations, and languages. The king wanted one act of worship to unite them all. The music was the signal. The instruments were a full royal orchestra: horns, pipes, stringed instruments like the lyre, harp and trigon (a small triangular harp), and the bagpipe. Notice how often the writer lists them. They appear four times in the chapter (vv. 5, 7, 10, 15), as regular as the music itself. Every time the band plays, everyone falls down.

Worship is often shaped this way. Powerful music, a great crowd and the pressure to join in can carry people along without thinking. The question is always: who is being worshipped?

And whoever does not fall down and worship shall immediately be cast into a burning fiery furnace."

Then came the threat. The furnace was probably a large kiln used for baking bricks or smelting metal, with an opening at the top for loading and a door at the side (v. 26). Babylon was a city of fired brick, so such furnaces were common. The punishment was designed to be public and terrifying.

Therefore, as soon as all the peoples heard the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, all the peoples, nations, and languages fell down and worshiped the golden image that King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.

As soon as the music sounded, everyone bowed. No one wanted to be the one left standing. Many of them no doubt believed in other gods, or in none. But bowing seemed a small price to pay for safety and a career.

The Bible shows that this scene will be repeated. In Revelation John sees a beast whose image demands worship and causes those who would not worship the image of the beast to be slain (Rev 13:15). Every age has its golden images: the state, success, money, pleasure, the opinion of the crowd. And every age asks believers whether they will bow when everyone else does. Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:21).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–18 — We Will Not Serve Your Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Certain Chaldeans accuse the Jews who refuse to bow (vv. 8-12). The enraged king gives Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego a second chance and taunts, who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands? (vv. 13-15). They answer that their God is able to deliver them, But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: True faith trusts God's power and obeys him whatever he chooses to do.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore at that time certain Chaldeans came forward and maliciously accused the Jews. They declared to King Nebuchadnezzar, "O king, live forever! You, O king, have made a decree, that every man who hears the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, shall fall down and worship the golden image. And whoever does not fall down and worship shall be cast into a burning fiery furnace. There are certain Jews whom you have appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men, O king, pay no attention to you; they do not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore at that time certain Chaldeans came forward and maliciously accused the Jews.

On a plain filled with thousands of bowing officials, three men were still standing. And someone noticed. Certain Chaldeans, members of the learned class, came forward to accuse them. The ESV's maliciously accused captures the idea that this was personal. These three Jews had been promoted over the province of Babylon (2:49), and their rivals saw an opportunity.

They declared to King Nebuchadnezzar, "O king, live forever!

You, O king, have made a decree, that every man who hears the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, shall fall down and worship the golden image.

And whoever does not fall down and worship shall be cast into a burning fiery furnace.

There are certain Jews whom you have appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These men, O king, pay no attention to you; they do not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up."

The accusers are clever. They flatter the king, quote his own decree back to him and then remind him that he himself had promoted these men: whom you have appointed. The charge is presented as ingratitude and disloyalty. These men, O king, pay no attention to you. That was not true. The three had served the king faithfully. They simply would not worship his gods.

Christians are often accused in the same way. Refusing to join in what everyone else does is described as hatred, arrogance or disloyalty. But there is a difference between refusing to worship a ruler and refusing to respect him. These men gave the king their work and their honor. They would not give him their worship.

Where was Daniel? The text does not say. He may have been away on the king's business, or his high position at court may have excused him from attending. We are not told, and it is better not to guess. The story is about these three men and their God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nebuchadnezzar in furious rage commanded that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be brought. So they brought these men before the king. Nebuchadnezzar answered and said to them, "Is it true, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods or worship the golden image that I have set up? Now if you are ready when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, to fall down and worship the image that I have made, well and good. But if you do not worship, you shall immediately be cast into a burning fiery furnace. And who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Nebuchadnezzar in furious rage commanded that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego be brought. So they brought these men before the king.

Nebuchadnezzar answered and said to them, "Is it true, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods or worship the golden image that I have set up?

The king is in a furious rage, but he does not execute them immediately. Perhaps he valued them as officials. Perhaps he could not believe that anyone would defy him. He asks, Is it true? as if giving them a chance to deny it.

Now if you are ready when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, lyre, trigon, harp, bagpipe, and every kind of music, to fall down and worship the image that I have made, well and good. But if you do not worship, you shall immediately be cast into a burning fiery furnace. And who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?"

The king offers a second chance. The band will play again. All they need to do is bow once. (The ESV notes that the words well and good are not in the Aramaic. The sentence simply breaks off, as angry people's sentences often do, and the meaning is plain.) This is the most dangerous kind of temptation, the one that comes with a reasonable offer: just once, just outwardly, and everything will be forgiven.

Then comes the king's real challenge: who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands? Over a century earlier the Assyrian king Sennacherib had mocked Jerusalem with almost the same words: Who among all the gods of the lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand? (2 Kgs 18:35). God answered Sennacherib by destroying his army. Nebuchadnezzar has forgotten that in chapter 2 he himself confessed that Daniel's God was God of gods and Lord of kings (2:47). Now he claims that no god can match him. The stage is set for God to answer the question.

verseByVerse.quote: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered and said to the king, "O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered and said to the king, "O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter.

Their answer is calm and short. We have no need to answer you in this matter. They are not being rude. They mean that there is nothing to discuss and no defense to prepare. The question had been settled long before the music played. They will not ask for more time or try to find a clever compromise. Their decision was made in their hearts, just as Daniel's was in 1:8.

If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king.

This verse is not easy to translate, and the ESV notes another possible reading: "If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, he will deliver us from the burning fiery furnace and out of your hand, O king." In that reading the "if" is not a doubt about God's power. It answers the king's challenge: if it comes to a contest of power between you and our God, then our God will deliver us. Either way, the three men are confident of two things. God is able, and God will rescue them out of your hand, whether by saving them from the fire or by taking them through death into his presence. Either way the king will not have the last word.

But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up."

Here are three of the bravest words in the Bible: But if not. They do not know whether God will keep them alive. They believe he can. They do not claim a promise that he will. But their obedience does not depend on the outcome. Even if God lets them burn, they will not bow.

This is the difference between faith and bargaining. Bargaining says, "I will serve God if he protects me." Faith says, "I will serve God because he is God, and I trust him with whatever he decides." Job said it this way: Though he slay me, I will hope in him (Job 13:15). The apostles said it before their own rulers: We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).

Christians today may not face a literal furnace, though many around the world do. But every believer will face moments where faithfulness costs something: a job, a friendship, a reputation, comfort. In those moments we need both halves of this answer. God is able. And even if he does not deliver us in the way we hope, we will not bow. And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matt 10:28). Hebrews honors both kinds of faithful people: those who quenched the power of fire (Heb 11:34), and those who were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life (Heb 11:35).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — Four Men in the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The furious king has the furnace heated seven times hotter; the three are bound and thrown in, and the flames kill the soldiers who throw them (vv. 19-23). Then the astonished king sees four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and the fourth like a son of the gods (vv. 24-25). He calls them out, and all his officials see that the fire had no power over them; no smell of fire had come upon them (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not always keep his people out of the fire, but he goes with them into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more than it was usually heated. And he ordered some of the mighty men of his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace. Then these men were bound in their cloaks, their tunics, their hats, and their other garments, and they were thrown into the burning fiery furnace. Because the king's order was urgent and the furnace overheated, the flame of the fire killed those men who took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell bound into the burning fiery furnace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Nebuchadnezzar was filled with fury, and the expression of his face was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. He ordered the furnace heated seven times more than it was usually heated.

The king's face twists with rage. A few minutes earlier he was offering a second chance. Now he is out of control. Seven times more means as hot as it could possibly be made. It was a senseless order. A hotter fire would not make them any more dead. But proud men who are defied rarely act wisely. The man who ruled the world could not rule his own temper.

And he ordered some of the mighty men of his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, and to cast them into the burning fiery furnace.

Then these men were bound in their cloaks, their tunics, their hats, and their other garments, and they were thrown into the burning fiery furnace.

They were thrown in fully dressed, in all their official clothes. (The ESV notes that the exact meaning of the words for cloaks and tunics is uncertain.) The detail matters later. Clothing burns easily, and these garments would be the first things the fire consumed.

Because the king's order was urgent and the furnace overheated, the flame of the fire killed those men who took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.

The king's fury killed his own soldiers. The flames were so fierce that the men who threw the prisoners in died at the opening. This shows the reader that the fire was real. There was no trick and no cool corner of the furnace. Anyone who came near it died.

And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell bound into the burning fiery furnace.

The sentence is slow and heavy. These three men... fell bound. It seems that the story is over. The idol has won. The faithful are gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished and rose up in haste. He declared to his counselors, "Did we not cast three men bound into the fire?" They answered and said to the king, "True, O king." He answered and said, "But I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are not hurt; and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished and rose up in haste. He declared to his counselors, "Did we not cast three men bound into the fire?" They answered and said to the king, "True, O king."

Suddenly the king jumps up from his seat. He cannot believe what he sees. He checks with his advisers: we threw in three men, tied up, didn't we? True, O king.

He answered and said, "But I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and they are not hurt; and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods."

Everything about the scene has changed. Not three but four. Not bound but unbound. Not falling but walking, as calmly as if they were in a garden. Not burned but not hurt. The only thing the fire destroyed was the ropes that tied them.

Who was the fourth man? Nebuchadnezzar, a pagan, describes him in pagan terms: like a son of the gods, meaning a divine or heavenly being. In verse 28 he calls him God's angel. Christians have understood this in two ways. Some believe that God sent an angel, as he did for Daniel in the lions' den (6:22). Many others, in the Reformed tradition and long before it, believe that this was an appearance of the Son of God himself before he was born in Bethlehem, like the angel of the LORD who appeared to Moses in a flame of fire in a bush that was not consumed (Exod 3:2). The text does not settle the question, and faithful Christians hold both views.

But the heart of the matter is the same either way. God did not keep his servants out of the fire. He met them in it. Long before, God had promised: when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you (Isa 43:2). And the risen Christ has promised every believer the same presence: behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age (Matt 28:20). Believers are not promised a life without furnaces. They are promised that they will never be in the furnace alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the door of the burning fiery furnace; he declared, "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here!" Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out from the fire. And the satraps, the prefects, the governors, and the king's counselors gathered together and saw that the fire had not had any power over the bodies of those men. The hair of their heads was not singed, their cloaks were not harmed, and no smell of fire had come upon them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the door of the burning fiery furnace; he declared, "Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, servants of the Most High God, come out, and come here!" Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego came out from the fire.

The king who had asked who is the god who will deliver you? now comes to the door of the furnace and calls them servants of the Most High God. The title Most High means the God above all gods. It will become one of the most important names for God in the book. The contest of verse 15 is over, and the king has announced the winner himself.

And the satraps, the prefects, the governors, and the king's counselors gathered together and saw that the fire had not had any power over the bodies of those men. The hair of their heads was not singed, their cloaks were not harmed, and no smell of fire had come upon them.

The same officials who had bowed before the image now crowd around three men and inspect them. Everything is examined, and the evidence is overwhelming. Their bodies were untouched. Their hair was not even singed. Their cloaks were unharmed. And there was not even the smell of fire on them. Anyone who has stood near a bonfire knows how the smoke gets into your clothes. These men walked out of a blazing furnace smelling of nothing at all.

God's deliverance was complete. And the whole government of Babylon became witnesses to it. The very crowd that had been gathered to worship an idol ended up seeing the power of the living God.

For those who belong to Christ, this is a picture of something greater still. The fire that no human being can survive is the judgment of God against sin. Jesus did not walk through that fire untouched. He took it upon himself on the cross, so that all who trust him would come through it without even the smell of fire upon them. Through his death he delivered all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–30 — No Other God Who Is Able to Rescue
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar blesses the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, who has sent his angel and delivered his servants, who trusted in him (v. 28). He decrees death for anyone who speaks against their God, for there is no other god who is able to rescue in this way, and promotes the three (vv. 29-30).
verseByVerse.theology: God's rescue of his faithful servants compels even their enemies to acknowledge him.

verseByVerse.quote: Nebuchadnezzar answered and said, "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel and delivered his servants, who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command, and yielded up their bodies rather than serve and worship any god except their own God. Therefore I make a decree: Any people, nation, or language that speaks anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be torn limb from limb, and their houses laid in ruins, for there is no other god who is able to rescue in this way." Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nebuchadnezzar answered and said, "Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who has sent his angel and delivered his servants, who trusted in him, and set aside the king's command, and yielded up their bodies rather than serve and worship any god except their own God.

The king's words are a remarkable summary of the chapter. He praises the God who has sent his angel and delivered his servants. And he describes their faith accurately. They trusted in him. They set aside the king's command (the ESV notes that the Aramaic says they "changed" it, as if their obedience to God overruled the king's word). And they yielded up their bodies, choosing to die rather than to worship anyone but God.

That is what the New Testament asks of every Christian: present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship (Rom 12:1). The three offered their bodies to the fire. God gave them back. Our bodies belong to him too, in life and in death.

Therefore I make a decree: Any people, nation, or language that speaks anything against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be torn limb from limb, and their houses laid in ruins, for there is no other god who is able to rescue in this way."

The king has learned something, but not enough. He admits that there is no other god who is able to rescue in this way. Yet his response is to threaten violence, the same method he used to force people to worship his image. He still thinks faith can be commanded by decree. He honors the God of the three men, but he does not yet bow to him as his own God. That will take another humbling, in chapter 4.

We should not be surprised when people are impressed by God's power without surrendering their lives to him. Admiration is not conversion. One day every knee should bow... and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil 2:10-11). The question is whether we bow now in faith, or later when it is too late.

Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the province of Babylon.

The chapter ends where chapter 2 ended, with God's faithful servants lifted up. The men who were thrown down into the fire are raised up in the kingdom. That is the pattern of the whole Bible, and it reaches its fullest form in Christ, who went down into death and was raised and exalted above every name. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world (John 16:33).

3.title: But If Not
3.overview:
Nebuchadnezzar sets up an image of gold sixty cubits high on the plain of Dura and gathers all the officials of his provinces to its dedication. A herald commands all peoples, nations and languages to fall down and worship the image when they hear the music, or be thrown into a burning fiery furnace, and all the peoples bow (vv. 1-7).

Certain Chaldeans accuse the Jews, reporting that Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego do not serve the king's gods or worship the image. The enraged king offers them another chance and asks who the god is who will deliver them from his hands. They answer that they need not defend themselves; their God is able to deliver them, but if not, they still will not serve his gods or worship the image (vv. 8-18).

The furious king orders the furnace heated seven times hotter, and the three are bound and thrown in; the flames kill the men who throw them. Then the astonished king sees four men unbound, walking in the fire unhurt, and the fourth like a son of the gods. He calls the three out, and his officials see that the fire had no power over their bodies, their hair was not singed, and no smell of fire was on them (vv. 19-27).

Nebuchadnezzar blesses their God, who sent his angel and delivered his servants who trusted in him and yielded up their bodies rather than worship any other god. He decrees that anyone who speaks against their God will be torn limb from limb, for no other god is able to rescue in this way, and he promotes the three in the province of Babylon (vv. 28-30).
3.theology:
Idols are made by human hands, and every power that demands the worship belonging to God must be refused (vv. 1-7; Exod 20:3-5; Ps 115:4-8; Rev 13:15; 1 John 5:21).

Faithful believers may be maliciously accused, but they can honor rulers while refusing to worship them (vv. 8-12; Acts 5:29).

True faith trusts that God is able to deliver and obeys him even if he does not (vv. 16-18; Job 13:15; Matt 10:28; Heb 11:34-35).

God does not always keep his people out of the fire, but he is present with them in it (vv. 24-25; Isa 43:2; Matt 28:20).

God's deliverance is complete, and it points to Christ, who bore the fire of judgment so that his people are delivered from the fear of death (vv. 26-27; Heb 2:14-15).

Believers offer their bodies to God as living sacrifices (v. 28; Rom 12:1).

Admiring God's power is not the same as bowing to him in faith (vv. 28-29; Phil 2:10-11).
3.examples:
A ninety-foot golden statue on a flat plain.

A whole government bowing when the band plays.

Rivals who turn a matter of faith into a charge of disloyalty.

A second chance: just bow once.

"But if not."

Soldiers killed by the fire they stoked.

Four men walking loose in the flames.

Officials sniffing for smoke and finding none.

And you, O Belteshazzar, tell me the interpretation, because all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known to me the interpretation, but you are able, for the spirit of the holy gods is in you."<sup>19</sup>Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was dismayed for a while, and his thoughts alarmed him. The king answered and said, "Belteshazzar, let not the dream or the interpretation alarm you." Belteshazzar answered and said, "My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you and its interpretation for your enemies!<sup>20</sup>The tree you saw, which grew and became strong, so that its top reached to heaven, and it was visible to the end of the whole earth,<sup>21</sup>whose leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in which was food for all, under which beasts of the field found shade, and in whose branches the birds of the heavens lived—<sup>22</sup>it is you, O king, who have grown and become strong. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The King Tells His Dream
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nebuchadnezzar writes to all peoples to tell of the signs and wonders the Most High God has done for him (vv. 1-3). At ease in his palace, he dreamed of a great tree that reached to heaven and fed all the earth (vv. 4-12). A holy watcher came down and ordered it chopped down, leaving only a banded stump, and a man's mind changed to a beast's for seven periods of time, to the end that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men (vv. 13-17). The wise men could not interpret it, so the king told it to Daniel (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: God speaks even to proud rulers, warning them before he acts.

verseByVerse.quote: King Nebuchadnezzar to all peoples, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you! It has seemed good to me to show the signs and wonders that the Most High God has done for me. How great are his signs, how mighty his wonders! His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion endures from generation to generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Nebuchadnezzar to all peoples, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth: Peace be multiplied to you!

This chapter is unusual. It is written as an open letter from Nebuchadnezzar himself, the pagan king of Babylon, to his entire empire. Most of it is his personal testimony, told in his own words.

A small note for readers who compare Bibles: the ESV notes that in the original Aramaic these first three verses are counted as the end of chapter 3 (3:31-33), so Aramaic verse numbers in this chapter run three behind English ones. The words are the same. Only the numbering differs.

It has seemed good to me to show the signs and wonders that the Most High God has done for me.

How great are his signs, how mighty his wonders! His kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion endures from generation to generation.

The king begins where he will end, with praise. He has learned something he did not know in chapters 2 and 3. There he admired Daniel's God. Here he confesses that God's kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. His words sound almost exactly like the Psalms: Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and your dominion endures throughout all generations (Ps 145:13). The man who once built an image to celebrate his own kingdom now announces to the world that only one kingdom lasts forever. The rest of the chapter tells us how he learned it.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and prospering in my palace. I saw a dream that made me afraid. As I lay in bed the fancies and the visions of my head alarmed me. So I made a decree that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought before me, that they might make known to me the interpretation of the dream. Then the magicians, the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers came in, and I told them the dream, but they could not make known to me its interpretation. At last Daniel came in before me—he who was named Belteshazzar after the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods —and I told him the dream, saying, "O Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery is too difficult for you, tell me the visions of my dream that I saw and their interpretation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and prospering in my palace.

The story begins at the peak of his success. He was at ease and prospering. This is often the most dangerous moment in any life. Trouble drives people to God. Comfort can make them forget him. Jesus told of a rich man who said to himself, relax, eat, drink, be merry, and God said, Fool! This night your soul is required of you (Luke 12:19-20).

I saw a dream that made me afraid. As I lay in bed the fancies and the visions of my head alarmed me.

The king summoned all the wise men of Babylon (v. 6). Once again the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans and astrologers are summoned, and once again they could not make known to me its interpretation (v. 7). This time the king told them the dream. It made no difference. The problem was never lack of information. It was lack of access to the God who sends the dream.

At last Daniel came in before me, the king writes (v. 8). At last. Why did he try the wise men first, after all he had seen in chapter 2? Perhaps because Daniel's God made him uncomfortable. Proud people often turn to God only when everything else has failed.

The king introduces Daniel as he who was named Belteshazzar after the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods (v. 8). The king is still thinking as a polytheist. The ESV notes that the phrase could also be translated "Spirit of the holy God". Either way, he recognizes that Daniel has a wisdom that comes from heaven.

"O Belteshazzar, chief of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you and that no mystery is too difficult for you, tell me the visions of my dream that I saw and their interpretation.

verseByVerse.quote: The visions of my head as I lay in bed were these: I saw, and behold, a tree in the midst of the earth, and its height was great. The tree grew and became strong, and its top reached to heaven, and it was visible to the end of the whole earth. Its leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in it was food for all. The beasts of the field found shade under it, and the birds of the heavens lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The visions of my head as I lay in bed were these: I saw, and behold, a tree in the midst of the earth, and its height was great.

The tree grew and became strong, and its top reached to heaven, and it was visible to the end of the whole earth.

Its leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in it was food for all. The beasts of the field found shade under it, and the birds of the heavens lived in its branches, and all flesh was fed from it.

The ancient world often pictured a great king or empire as a great tree. Ezekiel had described Assyria in the same way: a cedar of towering height, its top among the clouds, with all the birds of the heavens nesting in its boughs (Ezek 31:3, 6). This tree stands at the center of the world, its top reaches heaven, and everyone lives under its shade.

We should notice that the picture is not all bad. Nebuchadnezzar's empire did bring order, food and protection to many peoples. God had given him real power, and he had used some of it for good. But the phrase its top reached to heaven is ominous. It recalls the tower of Babel, whose builders wanted a tower with its top in the heavens to make a name for themselves (Gen 11:4). A tree that grows toward heaven is a king who is starting to think he belongs there.

verseByVerse.quote: "I saw in the visions of my head as I lay in bed, and behold, a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven. He proclaimed aloud and said thus: 'Chop down the tree and lop off its branches, strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the beasts flee from under it and the birds from its branches. But leave the stump of its roots in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze, amid the tender grass of the field. Let him be wet with the dew of heaven. Let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth. Let his mind be changed from a man's, and let a beast's mind be given to him; and let seven periods of time pass over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I saw in the visions of my head as I lay in bed, and behold, a watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven.

A watcher is a heavenly messenger, one of God's angels who watch over the affairs of the earth. The king calls him a holy one. He comes from heaven with a message.

He proclaimed aloud and said thus: 'Chop down the tree and lop off its branches, strip off its leaves and scatter its fruit. Let the beasts flee from under it and the birds from its branches.

But leave the stump of its roots in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze, amid the tender grass of the field. Let him be wet with the dew of heaven. Let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth.

The great tree is cut down. But there is mercy in the sentence: leave the stump of its roots. The band of iron and bronze around the stump probably pictures protection, keeping the stump from being destroyed so that it can grow again. The judgment will not be the end.

Then, in the middle of the verse, the picture shifts from a tree to a man. Let him be wet with the dew of heaven. Let his portion be with the beasts. The dream is beginning to interpret itself. This tree is a person.

Let his mind be changed from a man's, and let a beast's mind be given to him; and let seven periods of time pass over him.

The man will lose his human mind and live like an animal. How long is seven periods of time? Many take it to mean seven years, but the text does not say. Seven in the Bible often suggests completeness. It will last exactly as long as God has decided, until his work in the king is complete.

verseByVerse.quote: The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, the decision by the word of the holy ones, to the end that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will and sets over it the lowliest of men.' This dream I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw. And you, O Belteshazzar, tell me the interpretation, because all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known to me the interpretation, but you are able, for the spirit of the holy gods is in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sentence is by the decree of the watchers, the decision by the word of the holy ones, to the end that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will and sets over it the lowliest of men.'

This is the key verse of the chapter, and perhaps of the whole book. The decision is announced by heavenly messengers, but Daniel will explain that it is really a decree of the Most High (v. 24). And its purpose is stated clearly: that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men.

Three truths are packed into that sentence. First, God rules over all human government. Second, he gives it to whom he will. No one holds power except by his gift. Third, he can set over it the lowliest of men. God is not impressed by human greatness. He can raise up the humble and bring down the proud whenever he chooses.

This is not only a lesson for Nebuchadnezzar. It is for the living, everyone who reads the story. Every president, prime minister, dictator and king holds office under the Most High. The LORD has established his throne in the heavens, and his kingdom rules over all (Ps 103:19). And in Jesus, God did exactly what this verse describes. He set over the world one who was born in a stable and died on a cross.

This dream I, King Nebuchadnezzar, saw. And you, O Belteshazzar, tell me the interpretation, because all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known to me the interpretation, but you are able, for the spirit of the holy gods is in you."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–27 — It Is You, O King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel is alarmed, but tells the king plainly: it is you, O king, who have grown and become strong (vv. 19-22). The king will be driven from people to live like an animal till you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men, but his kingdom will be restored once he knows that Heaven rules (vv. 23-26). Daniel urges him, break off your sins by practicing righteousness (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: Faithful love tells the truth and calls for repentance while there is still time.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was dismayed for a while, and his thoughts alarmed him. The king answered and said, "Belteshazzar, let not the dream or the interpretation alarm you." Belteshazzar answered and said, "My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you and its interpretation for your enemies! The tree you saw, which grew and became strong, so that its top reached to heaven, and it was visible to the end of the whole earth, whose leaves were beautiful and its fruit abundant, and in which was food for all, under which beasts of the field found shade, and in whose branches the birds of the heavens lived— it is you, O king, who have grown and become strong. Your greatness has grown and reaches to heaven, and your dominion to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was dismayed for a while, and his thoughts alarmed him. The king answered and said, "Belteshazzar, let not the dream or the interpretation alarm you." Belteshazzar answered and said, "My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you and its interpretation for your enemies!

Daniel understands the dream immediately, and it shocks him into silence. He is dismayed for a while. The meaning is terrible, and he must tell it to a king who has killed people for less.

But notice Daniel's heart. He does not rejoice that the king who destroyed Jerusalem is about to be judged. He says, may the dream be for those who hate you. Daniel genuinely cares about this man. After decades in his service, he wishes him well. That is what it means to seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf (Jer 29:7). Christians are told to pray for kings and all who are in high positions (1 Tim 2:2), including those who do not know God.

Daniel repeats the description of the tree (vv. 20-21), and then he says the hardest words of the chapter:

it is you, O king, who have grown and become strong. Your greatness has grown and reaches to heaven, and your dominion to the ends of the earth.

It is you, O king. Like Nathan telling David, "You are the man," Daniel does not soften the truth. Love that will not tell the truth is not love. Daniel is both kind and courageous. He speaks respectfully, but he speaks plainly.

verseByVerse.quote: And because the king saw a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven and saying, 'Chop down the tree and destroy it, but leave the stump of its roots in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze, in the tender grass of the field, and let him be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven periods of time pass over him,' this is the interpretation, O king: It is a decree of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king, that you shall be driven from among men, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field. You shall be made to eat grass like an ox, and you shall be wet with the dew of heaven, and seven periods of time shall pass over you, till you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will. And as it was commanded to leave the stump of the roots of the tree, your kingdom shall be confirmed for you from the time that you know that Heaven rules.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And because the king saw a watcher, a holy one, coming down from heaven and saying, 'Chop down the tree and destroy it, but leave the stump of its roots in the earth, bound with a band of iron and bronze, in the tender grass of the field, and let him be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven periods of time pass over him,'

this is the interpretation, O king: It is a decree of the Most High, which has come upon my lord the king,

Daniel makes sure the king knows who stands behind the watcher's words: It is a decree of the Most High. This is not fate, bad luck or the anger of Babylon's gods. It is the settled decision of the one true God.

that you shall be driven from among men, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field. You shall be made to eat grass like an ox, and you shall be wet with the dew of heaven, and seven periods of time shall pass over you, till you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will.

The punishment fits the sin. A king who has begun to think of himself as more than a man will be made less than a man. He who looked down on everyone will live on the ground with the cattle. The psalmist says, Man in his pomp yet without understanding is like the beasts that perish (Ps 49:20). Pride is a kind of madness, and God will let the king's outward life show what his heart has already become.

But notice the word till. The judgment has a goal: till you know that the Most High rules. God's aim is not to destroy Nebuchadnezzar but to bring him to his senses.

And as it was commanded to leave the stump of the roots of the tree, your kingdom shall be confirmed for you from the time that you know that Heaven rules.

The stump means hope. His kingdom will be given back to him once he learns the lesson. Daniel uses a striking phrase: Heaven rules. It is a reverent way of saying "God rules". Matthew's Gospel speaks of "the kingdom of heaven" in the same spirit. The kingdom that truly rules the world is the one that comes from above.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you: break off your sins by practicing righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed, that there may perhaps be a lengthening of your prosperity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable to you: break off your sins by practicing righteousness, and your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed, that there may perhaps be a lengthening of your prosperity."

Daniel does not stop at the interpretation. He preaches. The dream is a warning, and warnings are given so that people can turn. Break off your sins.

Notice what Daniel names. Nebuchadnezzar's great sin was pride, and its fruit was oppression. An empire like his was built by conquest, and conquest leaves many people crushed and poor. Daniel calls him to show it in his conduct: practicing righteousness and showing mercy to the oppressed. This is not a way of earning God's forgiveness. It is what real repentance looks like. John the Baptist said the same: Bear fruits in keeping with repentance (Luke 3:8). Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy (Prov 28:13).

Daniel promises nothing more than perhaps. He does not presume to know whether God will delay the judgment. But he knows that God delights to show mercy to those who turn. I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezek 33:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–33 — Is Not This Great Babylon?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Twelve months later, walking on his palace roof, the king boasts of the great Babylon he built by my mighty power and for the glory of my majesty (vv. 28-30). While the words are still in his mouth a voice from heaven announces the sentence, and immediately he is driven out to live among the beasts, eating grass like an ox (vv. 31-33).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride goes before a fall, and God can humble the greatest in a moment.

verseByVerse.quote: All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar. At the end of twelve months he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon, and the king answered and said, "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this came upon King Nebuchadnezzar.

At this point the letter changes voice. Much of it is in the king's own words, as "I". But the account of his madness is told about him in the third person (vv. 28-33), and he returns to "I" only when his reason returns (v. 34). It is as though, during those years, there was no "I" left to tell the story.

At the end of twelve months he was walking on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon,

Twelve months. God gave the king a whole year to take Daniel's warning to heart. That was patience, not forgetfulness. Or do you presume on the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? (Rom 2:4). A delay in judgment is always an invitation to repent. The king did not accept it.

and the king answered and said, "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built by my mighty power as a royal residence and for the glory of my majesty?"

Picture the scene. The king stands on the flat roof of his palace, looking out over one of the wonders of the ancient world: massive walls, glittering gates, temples, palaces and gardens. Much of it he had built or rebuilt. And he speaks to no one but himself.

Listen to the pronouns: which I have built by my mighty power... for the glory of my majesty. There is no mention of God, who had given him the kingdom, the power, and the might, and the glory (2:37). He has taken every gift of God and claimed it as his own achievement. What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it? (1 Cor 4:7).

This is the sin at the root of all sins. It does not need a golden statue. It can live quietly in the heart of anyone who looks at their career, family, ministry or home and thinks, "I built this."

verseByVerse.quote: While the words were still in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, "O King Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: The kingdom has departed from you, and you shall be driven from among men, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field. And you shall be made to eat grass like an ox, and seven periods of time shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will." Immediately the word was fulfilled against Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from among men and ate grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven till his hair grew as long as eagles' feathers, and his nails were like birds' claws.
verseByVerse.commentary:
While the words were still in the king's mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, "O King Nebuchadnezzar, to you it is spoken: The kingdom has departed from you,

God's answer came while the words were still in the king's mouth. The year of patience was over. One sentence of pride was the last one.

The same thing happened centuries later to King Herod. When the crowd cried that his voice was The voice of a god, and not of a man!, Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give God the glory (Acts 12:22-23). Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall (Prov 16:18).

and you shall be driven from among men, and your dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field. And you shall be made to eat grass like an ox, and seven periods of time shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will."

Immediately the word was fulfilled against Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven from among men and ate grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven till his hair grew as long as eagles' feathers, and his nails were like birds' claws.

The greatest king on earth now crawls in the fields, eating grass. His hair grows long and matted like feathers, and his nails like claws. Some have compared his condition to a rare mental illness in which a person believes he is an animal. But the Bible is not interested in the medical name. It tells us the cause. God did it, and God did it for a reason.

It is a terrible picture, and it is meant to be. This is what pride finally does to a human being. It makes us less than human. When we refuse to live as creatures under God, we do not become gods. We become beasts. The psalmist confessed his own bitterness toward God in the same way: I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you (Ps 73:22).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 34–37 — My Reason Returned to Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the end of the days the king lifts his eyes to heaven, his reason returns, and he blesses the Most High, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and none can stay his hand (vv. 34-35). He is restored to his kingdom (v. 36) and ends his proclamation: those who walk in pride he is able to humble (v. 37).
verseByVerse.theology: The humbled sinner who looks up to heaven finds his sanity and learns to praise the King of heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and praised and honored him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom endures from generation to generation; all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, "What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of the days I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my reason returned to me, and I blessed the Most High, and praised and honored him who lives forever, for his dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom endures from generation to generation;

Now the king speaks again as "I". Notice the order of events. First, I... lifted my eyes to heaven. Then, my reason returned to me. An animal looks down at the ground. A man made in God's image looks up. The moment he looked to heaven, he began to be human again.

That is what repentance is. It is coming to our senses. When the prodigal son sat among the pigs, he came to himself and said, I will arise and go to my father (Luke 15:17-18). Sin is madness. Turning to God is sanity. The king's first act as a sane man was worship: I blessed the Most High.

all the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing, and he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, "What have you done?"

The man who had said Is not this great Babylon? now says that all the earth's inhabitants, himself included, are accounted as nothing compared to God. Isaiah said the same: All the nations are as nothing before him (Isa 40:17). No one can stay his hand, that is, stop him, or demand that he explain himself. Paul asks, who are you, O man, to answer back to God? (Rom 9:20). This is not a gloomy thought. For those who trust God, it is the safest truth in the world. The one who cannot be stopped is the one who loves his people.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time my reason returned to me, and for the glory of my kingdom, my majesty and splendor returned to me. My counselors and my lords sought me, and I was established in my kingdom, and still more greatness was added to me. Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven, for all his works are right and his ways are just; and those who walk in pride he is able to humble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time my reason returned to me, and for the glory of my kingdom, my majesty and splendor returned to me. My counselors and my lords sought me, and I was established in my kingdom, and still more greatness was added to me.

Just as Daniel had said, the stump grew again. The king was restored, and still more greatness was added. God's judgment on him had been severe, but it was also merciful. God humbled him in order to lift him up.

Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and extol and honor the King of heaven, for all his works are right and his ways are just; and those who walk in pride he is able to humble.

The king's last words in the book are a confession of faith. He calls God the King of heaven, which is to say, the true King, above himself. He admits that God's dealings with him were right and just, even the years in the field. And he ends with the lesson of his own life: those who walk in pride he is able to humble.

Was Nebuchadnezzar truly converted? Christians have answered differently. Many believe his words show genuine faith. He now praises God as the everlasting King and accepts God's judgment on himself as just. Others are more cautious, noting that he still speaks of my majesty and splendor, and that we are not told he abandoned Babylon's gods. The Bible does not settle the question for us. What is certain is that God humbled the proudest man on earth and made him proclaim God's glory to the whole world.

The chapter's lesson is written across the whole Bible: God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11). And it points us to the one who walked the opposite path. Nebuchadnezzar grasped at glory and was brought down to the level of the beasts. Jesus Christ, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped. He humbled himself to the point of death on a cross, Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name (Phil 2:6-9). The way up in God's kingdom is always the way down. Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you (1 Pet 5:6).

4.title: The Most High Rules
4.overview:
King Nebuchadnezzar writes to all peoples, nations and languages to tell of the signs and wonders the Most High God has done for him, praising God's everlasting kingdom (vv. 1-3).

At ease in his palace, he had a frightening dream that his wise men could not interpret. He told it to Daniel: a great tree reaching to heaven, feeding all creatures, was ordered cut down by a holy watcher from heaven, leaving a stump bound with iron and bronze, and a man's mind was to be changed to a beast's for seven periods of time, so that the living may know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men (vv. 4-18).

Daniel, dismayed, explains that the tree is the king. He will be driven from men to live with the beasts and eat grass until he knows that the Most High rules, but his kingdom will be restored when he knows that Heaven rules. Daniel urges him to break off his sins by practicing righteousness and showing mercy to the oppressed (vv. 19-27).

Twelve months later, as the king boasts on his palace roof of the great Babylon he built by his own power and for his own glory, a voice from heaven pronounces the sentence, and he is immediately driven out to live like an animal (vv. 28-33).

At the end of the days he lifts his eyes to heaven, his reason returns, and he blesses the Most High, whose dominion is everlasting and whose hand none can stay. He is restored to his kingdom with greater greatness, and he praises the King of heaven, whose ways are just and who is able to humble those who walk in pride (vv. 34-37).
4.theology:
The Most High rules the kingdom of men, gives it to whom he will, and can set over it the lowliest of men (vv. 17, 25, 32; Ps 103:19).

God warns the proud before he judges them, and his patience is meant to lead to repentance (vv. 27, 29; Rom 2:4; Ezek 33:11).

True repentance breaks off sin and bears fruit in righteousness and mercy to the oppressed (v. 27; Luke 3:8; Prov 28:13).

Pride claims God's gifts as one's own achievement, and it dehumanizes; God humbles the proud (vv. 30-33, 37; 1 Cor 4:7; Prov 16:18; Acts 12:23; Ps 49:20).

Looking up to God in humility restores true sanity and leads to worship (vv. 34-35; Luke 15:17-18).

God's servants love and pray for rulers even while telling them hard truths (vv. 19-22; Jer 29:7; 1 Tim 2:1-2).

Nebuchadnezzar's grasping pride is the opposite of Christ, who humbled himself and was exalted above every name (v. 37; Phil 2:6-9; Luke 14:11; Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:6).
4.examples:
A king at ease and prospering in his palace.

A great tree whose top reaches heaven.

A stump bound with iron and bronze, kept for regrowth.

A servant who wishes the bad news were for the king's enemies.

A year of patience, wasted.

"Is not this great Babylon, which I have built?"

A ruler eating grass in the fields.

A man who looks up to heaven and gets his mind back.
