And you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see or hear or know, but the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored.<sup>24</sup>"Then from his presence the hand was sent, and this writing was inscribed.<sup>25</sup>And this is the writing that was inscribed: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN.<sup>26</sup>This is the interpretation of the matter: MENE, God has numbered the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end;<sup>27</sup>TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting;<sup>28</sup>PERES, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians."<sup>29</sup>Then Belshazzar gave the command, and Daniel was clothed with purple, a chain of gold was put around his neck, and a proclamation was made about him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom.<sup>30</sup>That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed.<sup>31</sup>And Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — A Feast and a Hand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: King Belshazzar holds a great feast for a thousand lords and, drinking, orders the gold and silver vessels from the temple in Jerusalem brought so that he and his guests can drink from them while praising their idols (vv. 1-4). Immediately the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall, and the terrified king offers purple, a gold chain and the rank of third ruler to anyone who can read it, but his wise men cannot (vv. 5-9).
verseByVerse.theology: God will not be mocked, and his judgment can interrupt the proudest celebration in an instant.

verseByVerse.quote: King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his lords and drank wine in front of the thousand. Belshazzar, when he tasted the wine, commanded that the vessels of gold and of silver that Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple in Jerusalem be brought, that the king and his lords, his wives, and his concubines might drink from them. Then they brought in the golden vessels that had been taken out of the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem, and the king and his lords, his wives, and his concubines drank from them. They drank wine and praised the gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his lords and drank wine in front of the thousand.

Chapter 5 jumps forward more than twenty years. Nebuchadnezzar died in 562 BC, and several short reigns followed. By now the last king of Babylon was a man named Nabonidus, who spent years away from the capital. He left his son Belshazzar in charge of the city. So Belshazzar ruled Babylon, but under his father. That detail will explain something important later in the chapter.

The date is October 539 BC. The armies of the Medes and Persians, led by Cyrus, were already in the region and had defeated Babylon's forces nearby. And in the city, Belshazzar threw a party. Ancient historians later recorded that Babylon fell while its people were celebrating a festival. The king was drinking in front of the thousand, showing off, as if nothing could touch him.

Belshazzar, when he tasted the wine, commanded that the vessels of gold and of silver that Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken out of the temple in Jerusalem be brought, that the king and his lords, his wives, and his concubines might drink from them.

Notice the words when he tasted the wine. The drink loosened whatever restraint he had left. He called for the sacred vessels from God's temple, the same ones we saw carried to Babylon in 1:2. For almost seventy years they had sat in a treasury. Now the king used them as party cups.

The ESV notes that father can also mean "predecessor". In the ancient world a king often called an earlier king his "father" even when they were not closely related. Nebuchadnezzar was Belshazzar's great predecessor on the throne of Babylon.

Then they brought in the golden vessels that had been taken out of the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem, and the king and his lords, his wives, and his concubines drank from them.

They drank wine and praised the gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone.

This was not merely bad manners. It was deliberate contempt. They drank from the vessels of the living God while praising idols. It was as if to say, "Look what our gods did to the God of Israel. His holy things are now our drinking cups." With an enemy army at the gates, Belshazzar chose to mock the God who rules history.

The prophets had seen this night coming. Isaiah described Babylon's leaders at a feast: They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield! (Isa 21:5). And Jeremiah said that God would punish Babylon with the vengeance for his temple (Jer 51:11). Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall of the king's palace, opposite the lampstand. And the king saw the hand as it wrote. Then the king's color changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall of the king's palace, opposite the lampstand. And the king saw the hand as it wrote.

Immediately. God did not wait. In the middle of the laughter, a hand appeared, just the fingers of a hand, and began to write on the wall. It wrote opposite the lampstand, where the light was brightest and everyone could see it. And the king saw it moving.

Then the king's color changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; his limbs gave way, and his knees knocked together.

The proud king's face went white. His legs gave out. His knees knocked together. A few moments before he was mocking the God of Israel. Now he could not stand up. That is how quickly human arrogance collapses when God acts. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb 10:31).

verseByVerse.quote: The king called loudly to bring in the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers. The king declared to the wise men of Babylon, "Whoever reads this writing, and shows me its interpretation, shall be clothed with purple and have a chain of gold around his neck and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom." Then all the king's wise men came in, but they could not read the writing or make known to the king the interpretation. Then King Belshazzar was greatly alarmed, and his color changed, and his lords were perplexed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king called loudly to bring in the enchanters, the Chaldeans, and the astrologers. The king declared to the wise men of Babylon, "Whoever reads this writing, and shows me its interpretation, shall be clothed with purple and have a chain of gold around his neck and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom."

The frightened king offers enormous rewards: royal purple, a gold chain and a place as the third ruler in the kingdom. Why third and not second? Because Belshazzar himself was only second. His father Nabonidus was still the king. The best Belshazzar could offer was the next place below himself. This small detail fits exactly what we know of Babylon's history in its final years.

Then all the king's wise men came in, but they could not read the writing or make known to the king the interpretation.

Then King Belshazzar was greatly alarmed, and his color changed, and his lords were perplexed.

For the third time in the book, Babylon's wise men fail (2:10-11; 4:7). They could not even read the words, let alone explain them. The words may have been written in a way they could not make sense of, or God may simply have hidden their meaning from them. Either way, all the learning of Babylon was useless in the one moment it was needed. The party became a scene of panic.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — There Is a Man in Your Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The queen reminds the king of Daniel, in whom Nebuchadnezzar found light and understanding and wisdom like the wisdom of the gods (vv. 10-12). Daniel is brought in, and the king repeats his offer of honors if he can read the writing and interpret it (vv. 13-16).
verseByVerse.theology: God's faithful servant may be forgotten by the powerful, but he is not forgotten by God.

verseByVerse.quote: The queen, because of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banqueting hall, and the queen declared, "O king, live forever! Let not your thoughts alarm you or your color change. There is a man in your kingdom in whom is the spirit of the holy gods. In the days of your father, light and understanding and wisdom like the wisdom of the gods were found in him, and King Nebuchadnezzar, your father—your father the king— made him chief of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and astrologers, because an excellent spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve problems were found in this Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar. Now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The queen, because of the words of the king and his lords, came into the banqueting hall, and the queen declared, "O king, live forever! Let not your thoughts alarm you or your color change.

The ESV notes that queen may mean "queen mother". That fits well. Belshazzar's wives were already at the feast (v. 2), but this woman comes in from outside, hearing the uproar, and she remembers the days of Nebuchadnezzar. She was likely an older woman of the royal family who had known that earlier reign.

There is a man in your kingdom in whom is the spirit of the holy gods. In the days of your father, light and understanding and wisdom like the wisdom of the gods were found in him, and King Nebuchadnezzar, your father—your father the king— made him chief of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and astrologers,

There is a man in your kingdom. Daniel had been forgotten. The man who once ruled the province of Babylon and served Nebuchadnezzar for decades was no longer part of the court. The new rulers had pushed him aside. But the queen remembered.

God's servants are often forgotten by the powerful. Faithful people spend years out of the spotlight. But God knows exactly where they are, and when he needs them, he brings them back.

because an excellent spirit, knowledge, and understanding to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve problems were found in this Daniel, whom the king named Belteshazzar. Now let Daniel be called, and he will show the interpretation."

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel was brought in before the king. The king answered and said to Daniel, "You are that Daniel, one of the exiles of Judah, whom the king my father brought from Judah. I have heard of you that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that light and understanding and excellent wisdom are found in you. Now the wise men, the enchanters, have been brought in before me to read this writing and make known to me its interpretation, but they could not show the interpretation of the matter. But I have heard that you can give interpretations and solve problems. Now if you can read the writing and make known to me its interpretation, you shall be clothed with purple and have a chain of gold around your neck and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Daniel was brought in before the king. The king answered and said to Daniel, "You are that Daniel, one of the exiles of Judah, whom the king my father brought from Judah.

Daniel is now an old man, probably in his eighties. He was a teenager when he was brought to Babylon. And notice how Belshazzar greets him: one of the exiles of Judah. Even after a lifetime of service, to this king Daniel is still a foreign captive. There may be a sneer in the words.

I have heard of you that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that light and understanding and excellent wisdom are found in you.

Now the wise men, the enchanters, have been brought in before me to read this writing and make known to me its interpretation, but they could not show the interpretation of the matter.

But I have heard that you can give interpretations and solve problems. Now if you can read the writing and make known to me its interpretation, you shall be clothed with purple and have a chain of gold around your neck and shall be the third ruler in the kingdom."

The king repeats his offer. He believes that anyone can be bought. He has spent the evening treating holy things as if they were his to use as he pleased. Now he assumes God's servant has a price too.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — You Have Not Humbled Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let your gifts be for yourself, Daniel answers, but he will read the writing (v. 17). He reminds the king how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind (vv. 18-21). And you his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this; he has defiled God's vessels and praised idols, but the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored (vv. 22-24).
verseByVerse.theology: To sin against the light we have been given is a grave sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel answered and said before the king, "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation. O king, the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship and greatness and glory and majesty. And because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed, and whom he would, he kept alive; whom he would, he raised up, and whom he would, he humbled. But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down from his kingly throne, and his glory was taken from him. He was driven from among the children of mankind, and his mind was made like that of a beast, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys. He was fed grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind and sets over it whom he will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Daniel answered and said before the king, "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation.

Daniel's reply is blunt. Let your gifts be for yourself. He is not rude, but he is not interested. His message is not for sale. The prophet Elisha refused Naaman's gifts in the same way: As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will receive none (2 Kgs 5:16). And Jesus told his disciples, You received without paying; give without pay (Matt 10:8). A servant of God who can be bought cannot be trusted to tell the truth.

Besides, Daniel knew something the king did not. By morning Babylon's honors would be worthless.

O king, the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar your father kingship and greatness and glory and majesty.

And because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed, and whom he would, he kept alive; whom he would, he raised up, and whom he would, he humbled.

Before Daniel reads the writing, he preaches. He begins with history. Nebuchadnezzar was the greatest king the world had seen, with the power of life and death over everyone. But all of it was given to him by the Most High God.

But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down from his kingly throne, and his glory was taken from him.

He was driven from among the children of mankind, and his mind was made like that of a beast, and his dwelling was with the wild donkeys. He was fed grass like an ox, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind and sets over it whom he will.

Daniel retells chapter 4 in a few sentences. The lesson was simple: God humbled the proudest king on earth until he knew that the Most High God rules. Nebuchadnezzar learned it, and he was restored.

verseByVerse.quote: And you his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this, but you have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven. And the vessels of his house have been brought in before you, and you and your lords, your wives, and your concubines have drunk wine from them. And you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see or hear or know, but the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored. "Then from his presence the hand was sent, and this writing was inscribed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this,

Here is the charge that seals Belshazzar's fate: though you knew all this. He was not ignorant. He knew what had happened to Nebuchadnezzar. The story had been proclaimed to the whole empire (4:1). He had the warning, and he ignored it. (The ESV notes that son can mean "successor", just as father can mean predecessor.)

Sinning in ignorance is serious. Sinning against knowledge is worse. Jesus said, Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required (Luke 12:48). That should sober every person who has grown up hearing the gospel. Knowing the truth does not save anyone. Only humbling ourselves before it does. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb 3:15).

but you have lifted up yourself against the Lord of heaven. And the vessels of his house have been brought in before you, and you and your lords, your wives, and your concubines have drunk wine from them. And you have praised the gods of silver and gold, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone, which do not see or hear or know, but the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored.

Daniel names the sins: pride against God, contempt for holy things and the worship of idols that do not see or hear or know. And then he puts his finger on the deepest sin of all: the God in whose hand is your breath... you have not honored.

Think about that. Every breath Belshazzar took that night, every mouthful of wine and every word of praise to his idols, was given to him by the God he mocked. That is true of every human being. God himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything (Acts 17:25). The heart of sin is not only doing bad things. It is living on God's gifts while refusing to honor the giver.

"Then from his presence the hand was sent, and this writing was inscribed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–31 — MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writing is interpreted: God has numbered the days of the kingdom; you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting; the kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians (vv. 25-28). Daniel is honored as third ruler (v. 29). That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom (vv. 30-31).
verseByVerse.theology: God weighs every life, and his word of judgment comes true exactly as he says.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the writing that was inscribed: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN. This is the interpretation of the matter: MENE, God has numbered the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end; TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting; PERES, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is the writing that was inscribed: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN.

The words on the wall were short, and each one was a kind of pun. The ESV's notes explain the wordplay: each word sounds like a verb that carries part of the message.

This is the interpretation of the matter: MENE, God has numbered the days of your kingdom and brought it to an end;

MENE sounds like the Aramaic word for "numbered". God had counted Belshazzar's days, and the last one had arrived. Every kingdom, and every life, has a number of days, and God knows the number. The word is written twice, perhaps for emphasis: it is certain.

TEKEL, you have been weighed in the balances and found wanting;

TEKEL sounds like the word for "weighed". Picture a merchant's scale, with a weight on one side. God put Belshazzar on the scale, and he was too light. Found wanting means he did not measure up. He was all show and no substance. By him actions are weighed (1 Sam 2:3). In the balances they go up; they are together lighter than a breath (Ps 62:9).

This is the most searching sentence in the chapter, because it is true of all of us. If God put any of us on his scale, we would be found wanting. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Rom 3:23). The only hope for anyone weighed by God is to have another's weight placed on the scale. That is the gospel. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). Paul's great desire was to be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own (Phil 3:9). In Christ, those who were found wanting are found complete.

PERES, your kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians."

PERES is the singular form of PARSIN, and the ESV notes that it sounds like both "divided" and "Persia". It is a double wordplay. The kingdom is being broken up, and it is being handed to the Persians. The message was not a warning with time to repent. It was a verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Belshazzar gave the command, and Daniel was clothed with purple, a chain of gold was put around his neck, and a proclamation was made about him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom. That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed. And Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Belshazzar gave the command, and Daniel was clothed with purple, a chain of gold was put around his neck, and a proclamation was made about him, that he should be the third ruler in the kingdom.

Strangely, Belshazzar keeps his word and honors Daniel. But he shows no sign of repentance. He does not humble himself, pray or confess. He treats the message of God's judgment as a clever puzzle solved, not as a call to his knees. Daniel accepted the honors he had not asked for, but they would last only a few hours.

That very night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed.

The Medes and Persians entered the city that night, and Babylon, the head of gold, fell almost without a battle. The king who began the evening mocking God did not live to see the morning. The prophets had foretold it: Fallen, fallen is Babylon (Isa 21:9). Jeremiah had written that God would make Babylon's leaders drunk so that they would sleep a perpetual sleep and not wake (Jer 51:57).

Chapters 4 and 5 stand side by side on purpose. Two kings were both proud, and both were warned. One humbled himself and was restored. The other did not and was destroyed. He who is often reproved, yet stiffens his neck, will suddenly be broken beyond healing (Prov 29:1). The difference between them was not the size of their sins. It was what they did with God's warning. Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor 6:2).

And Darius the Mede received the kingdom, being about sixty-two years old.

A new ruler takes over Babylon. (The ESV notes that in the Aramaic this verse is counted as 6:1.) Who was Darius the Mede? No other ancient record we have mentions a ruler by that name, so Christians have offered different suggestions. Some believe he was a governor whom Cyrus appointed over Babylon. Others suggest that "Darius the Mede" was another title for Cyrus himself. We do not have enough evidence to be certain. What matters is that the kingdom passed exactly as the writing on the wall said it would, to the Medes and Persians.

And Daniel, the old exile, was still there. Babylon had fallen. The king who mocked God was dead. But God's servant was still standing. As 1:21 promised, Daniel was there, and the empire was not.

5.title: Weighed and Found Wanting
5.overview:
King Belshazzar holds a great feast for a thousand of his lords. When he has tasted the wine, he orders the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem to be brought, and he and his lords, wives and concubines drink from them while praising gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone. Immediately the fingers of a human hand write on the plaster of the wall, and the terrified king offers purple, a gold chain and the rank of third ruler to whoever can read and interpret it. His wise men cannot (vv. 1-9).

The queen tells the king about Daniel, in whom Nebuchadnezzar found an excellent spirit and wisdom to interpret dreams and solve problems. Daniel is brought in, and the king repeats his offer (vv. 10-16).

Daniel tells the king to keep his gifts but agrees to read the writing. He reminds him how the Most High God gave Nebuchadnezzar greatness and humbled him when he became proud, until he knew that God rules the kingdom of mankind. Belshazzar, though he knew all this, has not humbled his heart but has lifted himself up against the Lord of heaven, drunk from the vessels of his house and praised idols, and has not honored the God who holds his breath (vv. 17-24).

The writing is MENE, MENE, TEKEL, and PARSIN: God has numbered the days of the kingdom and ended it; the king has been weighed in the balances and found wanting; the kingdom is divided and given to the Medes and Persians. Daniel is clothed in purple and proclaimed third ruler. That very night Belshazzar is killed, and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom (vv. 25-31).
5.theology:
God is not mocked; contempt for what is holy brings his judgment, as the prophets foretold (vv. 1-6; Gal 6:7; Isa 21:5, 9; Jer 51:11, 57; Heb 10:31).

God's servants may be forgotten by the powerful but are kept by God for his purposes (vv. 10-13).

God's message cannot be bought (v. 17; 2 Kgs 5:16; Matt 10:8).

To sin against knowledge is especially serious; those who have heard the warnings must humble themselves (v. 22; Luke 12:48; Heb 3:15; Prov 29:1).

Every human being lives on God's gifts of life and breath and owes him honor (v. 23; Acts 17:25).

God numbers and weighs every life; all are found wanting, and the only hope is the righteousness of God in Christ (vv. 26-27; Rom 3:23; 2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9).

God's word of judgment comes true exactly as spoken, and kingdoms pass as he decrees (vv. 28, 30-31; 2 Cor 6:2).
5.examples:
A party thrown while an enemy army waits outside.

Temple vessels used as drinking cups.

Fingers writing on a wall by lamplight.

A king whose knees knock together.

An offer of third place because the king himself is second.

An old servant who says, "Keep your gifts."

A merchant's scale that shows a king too light.

A king who does not live until morning.

And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.<sup>4</sup>Then the high officials and the satraps sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel with regard to the kingdom, but they could find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him.<sup>5</sup>Then these men said, "We shall not find any ground for complaint against this Daniel unless we find it in connection with the law of his God."<sup>6</sup>Then these high officials and satraps came by agreement to the king and said to him, "O King Darius, live forever!<sup>7</sup>All the high officials of the kingdom, the prefects and the satraps, the counselors and the governors are agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce an injunction, that whoever makes petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions.<sup>8</sup>Now, O king, establish the injunction and sign the document, so that it cannot be changed, according to the law of the Medes and the Persians, which cannot be revoked."<sup>9</sup>Therefore King Darius signed the document and injunction.<sup>10</sup>When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went to his house where he had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.<sup>11</sup>Then these men came by agreement and found Daniel making petition and plea before his God.<sup>12</sup>Then they came near and said before the king, concerning the injunction, "O king! Did you not sign an injunction, that anyone who makes petition to any god or man within thirty days except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?" The king answered and said, "The thing stands fast, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be revoked."<sup>13</sup>Then they answered and said before the king, "Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, O king, or the injunction you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day."<sup>14</sup>Then the king, when he heard these words, was much distressed and set his mind to deliver Daniel. And he labored till the sun went down to rescue him.<sup>15</sup>Then these men came by agreement to the king and said to the king, "Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians that no injunction or ordinance that the king establishes can be changed."<sup>16</sup>Then the king commanded, and Daniel was brought and cast into the den of lions. The king declared to Daniel, "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!"<sup>17</sup>And a stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his lords, that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.<sup>18</sup>Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting; no diversions were brought to him, and sleep fled from him.<sup>19</sup>Then, at break of day, the king arose and went in haste to the den of lions.<sup>20</sup>As he came near to the den where Daniel was, he cried out in a tone of anguish. The king declared to Daniel, "O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?"<sup>21</sup>Then Daniel said to the king, "O king, live forever!<sup>22</sup>My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, and they have not harmed me, because I was found blameless before him; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm."<sup>23</sup>Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that Daniel be taken up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.<sup>24</sup>And the king commanded, and those men who had maliciously accused Daniel were brought and cast into the den of lions—they, their children, and their wives. And before they reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones in pieces.<sup>25</sup>Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: "Peace be multiplied to you.<sup>26</sup>I make a decree, that in all my royal dominion people are to tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and his dominion shall be to the end.<sup>27</sup>He delivers and rescues; he works signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, he who has saved Daniel from the power of the lions."<sup>28</sup>So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Darius sets 120 satraps over his kingdom and three high officials over them, including Daniel, who so distinguishes himself that the king plans to set him over the whole kingdom (vv. 1-3). His jealous colleagues can find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, except in connection with the law of his God (vv. 4-5). They persuade the king to sign an irrevocable injunction that for thirty days no one may pray to any god or man except the king, on pain of the lions' den (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: A faithful life leaves enemies nothing to attack but its faith.

verseByVerse.quote: It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom 120 satraps, to be throughout the whole kingdom; and over them three high officials, of whom Daniel was one, to whom these satraps should give account, so that the king might suffer no loss. Then this Daniel became distinguished above all the other high officials and satraps, because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It pleased Darius to set over the kingdom 120 satraps, to be throughout the whole kingdom;

Babylon has fallen, and a new empire rules. The Medes and Persians organized their huge territory carefully. Satraps were provincial governors, each responsible for a region. Over these 120 governors Darius set three senior officials to keep watch on them, so that the king might suffer no loss (v. 2). In other words, their job was to stop corruption and make sure the taxes reached the king.

and over them three high officials, of whom Daniel was one, to whom these satraps should give account, so that the king might suffer no loss.

Daniel was now an old man, probably over eighty. He had served the kings of Babylon for most of his life. When Babylon fell, a new king might easily have removed all of the old regime's officials. Instead Darius kept him and gave him high office. God had kept Daniel through the fall of an empire and placed him again at the center of power.

Then this Daniel became distinguished above all the other high officials and satraps, because an excellent spirit was in him. And the king planned to set him over the whole kingdom.

Daniel stood out. The reason given is an excellent spirit, which includes his ability, but also his character: his wisdom, honesty and steadiness. The king planned to make him, in effect, prime minister of the entire empire.

Christians should notice this. Daniel's faith did not make him a poor employee. It made him an outstanding one. Believers are not called to do their work carelessly because "only spiritual things matter". Excellent, honest work in a secular job is one of the ways God's people honor him in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the high officials and the satraps sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel with regard to the kingdom, but they could find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him. Then these men said, "We shall not find any ground for complaint against this Daniel unless we find it in connection with the law of his God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the high officials and the satraps sought to find a ground for complaint against Daniel with regard to the kingdom, but they could find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him.

Success brought envy. The other officials probably did not want a foreign Jew promoted over them, and they may also have feared an honest man who would stop them from filling their own pockets. So they began an investigation. They searched his work for anything they could use: a mistake, a bribe, a misused payment, a careless decision.

They found nothing. No error or fault was found in him. Imagine a lifetime of public service examined by people who wanted to find something, and coming out clean. That is a remarkable testimony.

This is what Peter asks of Christians: Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds (1 Pet 2:12). Paul tells Titus to live so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us (Titus 2:8). The world will still oppose believers. But let it be for their faith, not for their faults.

Then these men said, "We shall not find any ground for complaint against this Daniel unless we find it in connection with the law of his God."

What a thing for enemies to say. The only place they could attack Daniel was his devotion to God. Could that be said of us? If people who disliked us searched our lives, would the only thing they could find be our faith?

verseByVerse.quote: Then these high officials and satraps came by agreement to the king and said to him, "O King Darius, live forever! All the high officials of the kingdom, the prefects and the satraps, the counselors and the governors are agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce an injunction, that whoever makes petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions. Now, O king, establish the injunction and sign the document, so that it cannot be changed, according to the law of the Medes and the Persians, which cannot be revoked." Therefore King Darius signed the document and injunction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then these high officials and satraps came by agreement to the king and said to him, "O King Darius, live forever!

The ESV notes that came by agreement could also be translated "came thronging". Either way, the picture is of a crowd of officials pressing in on the king together, with a plan already agreed among themselves.

All the high officials of the kingdom, the prefects and the satraps, the counselors and the governors are agreed that the king should establish an ordinance and enforce an injunction, that whoever makes petition to any god or man for thirty days, except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions.

Their claim was a lie. All the high officials... are agreed. But there were only three high officials (v. 2), and one of them was Daniel, who had certainly not agreed. The conspirators flattered the king with a proposal that for thirty days he alone would receive prayers. For a new ruler trying to win the loyalty of a conquered people, it may have seemed like a harmless way of showing who was in charge.

But the trap was set for one man. They knew Daniel's habit of prayer. They knew he would not stop. And they built a law that would make his faithfulness a crime.

Now, O king, establish the injunction and sign the document, so that it cannot be changed, according to the law of the Medes and the Persians, which cannot be revoked."

The Persian empire had a rule that once the king signed a law and sealed it, even he could not cancel it. The book of Esther says the same about Persian royal decrees: an edict written in the name of the king and sealed with the king's ring cannot be revoked (Esth 8:8). The rule was meant to show that the king's word was absolute. In practice it meant that the king could be trapped by his own word.

Therefore King Darius signed the document and injunction.

Flattery works. Darius signed without asking the obvious questions: who suggested this, and why? Leaders who love praise are easily used by those who give it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — As He Had Done Previously
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went home and, at his open windows toward Jerusalem, got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously (v. 10). His enemies catch him and report him to the king (vv. 11-13). The distressed king labors till sunset to rescue him, but he is reminded that the law cannot be changed (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: Faithful prayer is a steady habit, kept openly when it becomes costly.

verseByVerse.quote: When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went to his house where he had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Daniel knew that the document had been signed, he went to his house where he had windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. He got down on his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he had done previously.

This one verse is the heart of the chapter, and every phrase matters.

When Daniel knew. He was not caught unaware. He knew exactly what the law said and what it would cost. He did not complain, organize a protest or flee the city.

He went to his house. He went where he always prayed. He did not stage a public demonstration in the street. But he did not hide either.

Windows in his upper chamber open toward Jerusalem. Why toward Jerusalem? Centuries earlier, when King Solomon dedicated the temple, he prayed that if Israel ever went into exile for their sins and prayed toward their land... the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name, God would hear them and forgive (1 Kgs 8:48-49). Jerusalem lay in ruins and the temple was gone, but Daniel was still leaning on God's promise to hear the prayers of his people in exile.

He got down on his knees three times a day. This was a settled rhythm of prayer, like the psalmist's: Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice (Ps 55:17). Daniel was not a man who prayed only in emergencies. His prayer life was already built before the crisis came.

And prayed and gave thanks. With the lions waiting, Daniel gave thanks. He did not only ask for rescue. He thanked God. That is faith. Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you (1 Thess 5:18).

As he had done previously. These may be the most important words of all. Daniel did not start praying because of the crisis, and he did not stop because of the crisis. He simply kept doing what he had always done. Courage in the great moment grows out of faithfulness in ten thousand ordinary ones.

Why did Daniel not simply close his windows or pray silently for thirty days? God hears silent prayers. But to change his lifelong habit at the moment the king demanded it would have been to accept that the king had authority over his worship. Daniel was a loyal servant of the king in everything else. Here he had to obey God rather than man. Jesus warned against praying in public that they may be seen by others (Matt 6:5). Daniel was not showing off. He was refusing to hide.

verseByVerse.quote: Then these men came by agreement and found Daniel making petition and plea before his God. Then they came near and said before the king, concerning the injunction, "O king! Did you not sign an injunction, that anyone who makes petition to any god or man within thirty days except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?" The king answered and said, "The thing stands fast, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be revoked." Then they answered and said before the king, "Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, O king, or the injunction you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then these men came by agreement and found Daniel making petition and plea before his God.

The conspirators came together to watch, and they found exactly what they expected. Daniel was making petition and plea before his God. Surely he was praying about the danger he was in, and perhaps for the king and for his enemies too.

Then they came near and said before the king, concerning the injunction, "O king! Did you not sign an injunction, that anyone who makes petition to any god or man within thirty days except to you, O king, shall be cast into the den of lions?" The king answered and said, "The thing stands fast, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be revoked."

Before they even name Daniel, they make the king confirm the law. The trap closes step by step. The thing stands fast, the king says, not yet knowing who it will catch.

Then they answered and said before the king, "Daniel, who is one of the exiles from Judah, pays no attention to you, O king, or the injunction you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day."

Their words are full of contempt. They do not call him the king's most trusted official. They call him one of the exiles from Judah, a foreigner. And they accuse him of disrespecting the king, which is the same false charge made against his friends in 3:12. Daniel had served the king faithfully. He simply would not pray to him.

Faithful believers are often accused of disloyalty when their only offense is loyalty to God. Jesus warned, If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (John 15:20). Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Tim 3:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king, when he heard these words, was much distressed and set his mind to deliver Daniel. And he labored till the sun went down to rescue him. Then these men came by agreement to the king and said to the king, "Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians that no injunction or ordinance that the king establishes can be changed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king, when he heard these words, was much distressed and set his mind to deliver Daniel. And he labored till the sun went down to rescue him.

Now the king understands what has happened. He has been tricked into condemning the man he trusted most. He is much distressed, angry with himself more than with Daniel. He spends the entire day trying to find a legal way out.

Then these men came by agreement to the king and said to the king, "Know, O king, that it is a law of the Medes and Persians that no injunction or ordinance that the king establishes can be changed."

At sunset the conspirators return and remind the king of his own law. The most powerful man in the empire cannot save the man he loves. His word has become a chain around him.

This scene has a striking parallel in the Gospels. Pilate, the Roman governor, knew that Jesus was innocent. I find no guilt in this man, he said (Luke 23:4). He tried again and again to release him, desiring to release Jesus (Luke 23:20). And like Darius, he knew why the accusers wanted him dead: it was out of envy that they had delivered him up (Matt 27:18). But in the end Pilate, too, gave in to the pressure. There is a great difference. Darius was trapped by a law. Pilate was trapped by his own cowardice. And behind both scenes stood the purposes of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — He Shut the Lions' Mouths
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Daniel is thrown into the den, and the king says, May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you! A stone is sealed over the mouth (vv. 16-17). After a sleepless night the king runs to the den at dawn and cries out (vv. 18-20). My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, Daniel answers (vv. 21-22). He is lifted out unharmed, because he had trusted in his God, and his accusers are thrown to the lions (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: God is able to deliver those who trust him, and his justice finally overtakes their enemies.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king commanded, and Daniel was brought and cast into the den of lions. The king declared to Daniel, "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!" And a stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his lords, that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king commanded, and Daniel was brought and cast into the den of lions. The king declared to Daniel, "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!"

A lions' den was probably a pit in the ground, with an opening at the top through which the victim was thrown. Kings kept lions for hunting and for display, and verse 24 shows that these were far from tame.

The king's last words to Daniel are a mixture of hope and helplessness: May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you! The pagan king had noticed what everyone around Daniel noticed. He served his God continually, not occasionally. And the king now pinned his hope on that God, because he himself could do nothing.

And a stone was brought and laid on the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his own signet and with the signet of his lords, that nothing might be changed concerning Daniel.

A stone was rolled over the opening, and it was sealed. Probably wet clay was pressed over the edges of the stone and stamped with the king's ring and the rings of his nobles. If anyone moved the stone, the broken seal would show it. The seal of the lords meant the king could not secretly rescue Daniel. The seal of the king meant the lords could not secretly make sure he died. No human hand could interfere. Whatever happened next would be God's doing alone.

Readers of the Gospels will recall another stone and another seal. After Jesus was crucified, his enemies made the tomb secure by sealing the stone and setting a guard (Matt 27:66). There, too, the seal proved only that no human being had anything to do with what happened on the morning that followed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting; no diversions were brought to him, and sleep fled from him. Then, at break of day, the king arose and went in haste to the den of lions. As he came near to the den where Daniel was, he cried out in a tone of anguish. The king declared to Daniel, "O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the king went to his palace and spent the night fasting; no diversions were brought to him, and sleep fled from him.

The contrast is almost humorous. In the pit, Daniel was with the lions. In the palace, the king was the one who could not rest. He refused food and entertainment and lay awake all night. There is no sign that Daniel spent the night in the same anxiety. The man in the den was in God's hands. The man on the throne was in torment.

Then, at break of day, the king arose and went in haste to the den of lions.

At the first light the king runs to the den, the ruler of the empire hurrying through the streets at dawn.

As he came near to the den where Daniel was, he cried out in a tone of anguish. The king declared to Daniel, "O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?"

The king calls out in anguish, afraid of the silence that might answer. But listen to how he now speaks of God: the living God. The Persian king uses the same title that the Bible uses for the true God, in contrast to lifeless idols. And his question is the question of the whole book: is this God able? Nebuchadnezzar had asked the same thing mockingly (3:15). Darius asks it in hope.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Daniel said to the king, "O king, live forever! My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, and they have not harmed me, because I was found blameless before him; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm." Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that Daniel be taken up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Daniel said to the king, "O king, live forever!

The voice from the pit is calm and courteous. Daniel greets the king who condemned him with respect and without bitterness. There is no "How could you?" Like his Lord after him, When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Pet 2:23).

My God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, and they have not harmed me, because I was found blameless before him; and also before you, O king, I have done no harm."

Daniel gives God all the credit: My God sent his angel. The lions were not tame, and they were not full. God himself closed their mouths. The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear him, and delivers them (Ps 34:7). The book of Hebrews remembers Daniel among the heroes of faith who stopped the mouths of lions (Heb 11:33).

And Daniel declares his innocence twice: blameless before him, and before the king, I have done no harm. He had broken the king's law, but he had not wronged the king. Obeying God rather than man is not disloyalty. It is the only true loyalty.

Then the king was exceedingly glad, and commanded that Daniel be taken up out of the den. So Daniel was taken up out of the den, and no kind of harm was found on him, because he had trusted in his God.

Daniel is lifted out, and no kind of harm was found on him. Just as in the furnace, the deliverance was complete.

The writer tells us why: because he had trusted in his God. It was not because Daniel was an extraordinary man, though he was. It was because he trusted God. Without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him (Heb 11:6).

We should be careful here. God does not promise that every faithful believer will be rescued from every lion. Many have died for their faith, and Hebrews honors them too. Paul, near the end of his life, could say, I was rescued from the lion's mouth, and in the next breath, The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom (2 Tim 4:17-18). He knew he would soon be executed. For the Christian, the final deliverance is always certain, whether God brings us out of the den in this life or through death into his presence.

And this story points beyond itself. Daniel was innocent, condemned through envy, put into a pit, sealed in with a stone, and brought out alive at dawn. Jesus was innocent, condemned through envy, put into a tomb and sealed in with a stone. But Jesus was not spared death. He went all the way into it, bearing the sins of his people. And on the third day, early in the morning, the stone was rolled away and he came out alive, because it was not possible for him to be held by it (Acts 2:24). Daniel was delivered from death. Christ conquered it. That is why those who trust him are safe even in the den.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king commanded, and those men who had maliciously accused Daniel were brought and cast into the den of lions—they, their children, and their wives. And before they reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones in pieces.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the king commanded, and those men who had maliciously accused Daniel were brought and cast into the den of lions—they, their children, and their wives. And before they reached the bottom of the den, the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones in pieces.

This verse is hard to read. The accusers suffered the fate they had planned for Daniel, and that is justice. Scripture often describes the wicked falling into the pit they dug for others. The lions were clearly not tame or full: they seized the men before they reached the bottom of the den. Daniel's survival was no accident.

But the king also threw in their wives and children. That was the practice of ancient Persian kings, who often destroyed a traitor's whole family. The Bible records it; it does not approve it. God's law for Israel said plainly, nor shall children be put to death because of their fathers. Each one shall be put to death for his own sin (Deut 24:16). The terrible end of those families shows how deeply the sin of a few leaders can wound the people who depend on them, and it reminds us that the justice of human kings, even when it punishes real wrongdoing, is never the perfect justice of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–28 — His Kingdom Shall Never Be Destroyed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Darius decrees that all his dominion must tremble before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, the God who delivers and rescues (vv. 25-27). So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The deliverance of one faithful servant proclaims the living God to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: "Peace be multiplied to you. I make a decree, that in all my royal dominion people are to tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and his dominion shall be to the end. He delivers and rescues; he works signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, he who has saved Daniel from the power of the lions."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then King Darius wrote to all the peoples, nations, and languages that dwell in all the earth: "Peace be multiplied to you.

The chapter ends as chapter 4 did, with a pagan king writing to the whole world. The thirty-day law demanded that everyone pray to the king. The new decree tells everyone to fear Daniel's God.

I make a decree, that in all my royal dominion people are to tremble and fear before the God of Daniel, for he is the living God, enduring forever; his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and his dominion shall be to the end.

He delivers and rescues; he works signs and wonders in heaven and on earth, he who has saved Daniel from the power of the lions."

Darius's confession sounds very much like the message of the whole book. God is the living God, unlike the dead idols of the nations. He is enduring forever, while kings and empires come and go. His kingdom shall never be destroyed, the very words Daniel spoke to Nebuchadnezzar about the stone that fills the earth (2:44). And He delivers and rescues.

One man's quiet faithfulness in his upstairs room led to a proclamation across an empire. Daniel did not set out to be a missionary to the Persian court. He set out to be faithful, and God made his faithfulness a testimony to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So this Daniel prospered during the reign of Darius and the reign of Cyrus the Persian.

The historical half of the book ends with a quiet summary. Daniel prospered. The man who entered Babylon as a captive teenager outlived Nebuchadnezzar, saw Babylon fall, survived the lions and served the kings of Persia with honor.

Readers who remember the question about Darius the Mede (see 5:31) will notice that this verse mentions him alongside Cyrus. Some take it as two rulers whose reigns overlapped; others take it as two names for the same king. Either way, the point is clear. Kings change. The faithful servant of God remains.

The first six chapters of Daniel have taught one lesson from many angles: the Most High rules, and he is able to keep those who trust him, even in Babylon. The rest of the book will lift our eyes to the future. The kingdoms of this world will grow more beastly and more hostile. But the lesson of the lions' den stands behind every vision. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah... has conquered (Rev 5:5).

6.title: The Living God, Enduring Forever
6.overview:
Darius sets 120 satraps over his kingdom and three high officials over them, one of whom is Daniel. Because of the excellent spirit in him Daniel is distinguished above them all, and the king plans to set him over the whole kingdom. His rivals seek grounds for complaint but find no fault in him, and they decide to find it in connection with the law of his God (vv. 1-5).

They come to the king claiming that all his officials agree he should establish an injunction, unchangeable under the law of the Medes and Persians, that anyone who petitions any god or man except the king for thirty days be cast into the den of lions. Darius signs it (vv. 6-9).

When Daniel knows the document has been signed, he goes home and, with his windows open toward Jerusalem, kneels three times a day to pray and give thanks as he had done before. His enemies find him praying and report him to the king, who is greatly distressed and labors until sunset to deliver him, but they remind him that the law cannot be changed (vv. 10-15).

Daniel is cast into the den, and the king says, "May your God, whom you serve continually, deliver you!" A stone is laid on the den and sealed. The king spends a sleepless night fasting, and at daybreak hurries to the den and calls out. Daniel answers that God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths because he was blameless. He is taken up unharmed because he trusted in his God, and his accusers, with their wives and children, are thrown to the lions (vv. 16-24).

Darius writes to all peoples that they must tremble before the God of Daniel, the living God whose kingdom shall never be destroyed, who delivers and rescues. Daniel prospers during the reigns of Darius and Cyrus the Persian (vv. 25-28).
6.theology:
Believers honor God by excellent, honest work, so that opponents can find no fault but their faith (vv. 3-5; 1 Pet 2:12; Titus 2:7-8).

Faithful prayer is a settled habit that does not stop when it becomes costly; God's people obey God rather than men while remaining loyal servants in everything else (vv. 10, 22; 1 Kgs 8:48-49; Ps 55:17; 1 Thess 5:17-18).

The godly will be falsely accused and persecuted, as their Lord was (vv. 5, 13; John 15:20; 2 Tim 3:12; Matt 27:18).

God is able to deliver those who trust in him, and his final deliverance of his people is certain even when he does not spare them from death (vv. 22-23; Ps 34:7; Heb 11:6, 33; 2 Tim 4:17-18).

Daniel's condemnation, sealed stone and dawn deliverance foreshadow Christ, who was condemned through envy, sealed in a tomb and raised from death (vv. 14-23; Luke 23:4, 20; Matt 27:66; Acts 2:24).

Human justice, even when it punishes real wrong, falls short of God's perfect justice (v. 24; Deut 24:16).

The living God endures forever, his kingdom shall never be destroyed, and he delivers and rescues (vv. 26-27; 2:44; Rev 5:5).
6.examples:
An investigation that finds a lifetime of work without a single fault.

A law written to make one man's prayers a crime.

Open windows facing a ruined city.

Prayer and thanksgiving "as he had done previously".

A king who works all day to undo his own signature.

A stone sealed with the rings of the king and his lords.

A sleepless king and a safe prisoner.

A man lifted from the den without a scratch.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream and visions of his head as he lay in his bed. Then he wrote down the dream and told the sum of the matter.<sup>2</sup>Daniel declared, "I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea.<sup>3</sup>And four great beasts came up out of the sea, different from one another.<sup>4</sup>The first was like a lion and had eagles' wings. Then as I looked its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man, and the mind of a man was given to it.<sup>5</sup>And behold, another beast, a second one, like a bear. It was raised up on one side. It had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and it was told, 'Arise, devour much flesh.'<sup>6</sup>After this I looked, and behold, another, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back.
