verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Four Beasts from the Sea
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the first year of Belshazzar, Daniel dreams of the four winds stirring up the great sea, and four great beasts came up out of the sea, different from one another (vv. 1-3): a lion with eagles' wings given a man's mind, a bear raised on one side with three ribs in its mouth, and a leopard with four wings and four heads (vv. 4-6). A fourth beast, terrifying, with iron teeth and ten horns, crushes everything, and a little horn with eyes and a boastful mouth uproots three of the horns (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Behind the glory of human empires lies a beastly, devouring power that sets itself against God.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream and visions of his head as he lay in his bed. Then he wrote down the dream and told the sum of the matter. Daniel declared, "I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea. And four great beasts came up out of the sea, different from one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream and visions of his head as he lay in his bed. Then he wrote down the dream and told the sum of the matter.

With chapter 7 the book changes. The first six chapters told stories about Daniel and his friends, mostly in the third person. The last six record visions that Daniel himself saw, told mostly in his own voice. The book is arranged by theme rather than strict date. This vision came in the first year of Belshazzar, years before Babylon fell in chapter 5. At that point Babylon still looked secure, and Daniel was probably in his sixties.

This chapter is the hinge of the whole book. It is still written in Aramaic (see the note at 2:4), so it belongs with chapters 2-6. But it looks forward to chapters 8-12. And it contains one of the most important prophecies in the Old Testament, one that Jesus applied to himself again and again.

Daniel declared, "I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were stirring up the great sea.

In the Bible the sea often pictures the restless, chaotic world of nations opposed to God. Isaiah wrote of the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters (Isa 17:12), and the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet (Isa 57:20). The four winds of heaven suggest that the storm comes from every direction, and that heaven is the one stirring it. Even the turmoil of world history is under God's hand.

And four great beasts came up out of the sea, different from one another.

Four beasts rise from the storm. Readers of chapter 2 will immediately think of the four metals of Nebuchadnezzar's statue. The two chapters describe the same four kingdoms, but from two different points of view. In chapter 2 a pagan king saw human empires as a glorious, shining statue. In chapter 7 God's prophet sees them as they really are: wild, devouring beasts. What the world admires, heaven sees as monstrous.

verseByVerse.quote: The first was like a lion and had eagles' wings. Then as I looked its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man, and the mind of a man was given to it. And behold, another beast, a second one, like a bear. It was raised up on one side. It had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and it was told, 'Arise, devour much flesh.' After this I looked, and behold, another, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back. And the beast had four heads, and dominion was given to it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first was like a lion and had eagles' wings. Then as I looked its wings were plucked off, and it was lifted up from the ground and made to stand on two feet like a man, and the mind of a man was given to it.

The first beast is Babylon, the head of gold. The lion was the king of beasts, and the eagle the king of birds, a fitting image for Nebuchadnezzar's mighty and swift empire. Jeremiah pictured Babylon's attack as a lion leaving its thicket (Jer 4:7), and Ezekiel pictured the king of Babylon as a great eagle (Ezek 17:3, 12). Babylon itself decorated its great processional way with images of lions.

Then something strange happens. The wings are torn off, and the beast stands up like a man and receives the mind of a man. This probably recalls chapter 4, where Nebuchadnezzar lost his human mind, lived like a beast and then had his reason restored. The proud lion was humbled and made human again.

And behold, another beast, a second one, like a bear. It was raised up on one side. It had three ribs in its mouth between its teeth; and it was told, 'Arise, devour much flesh.'

The second beast matches the silver of chapter 2: the empire of the Medes and Persians. The bear is raised up on one side, probably because the empire had two partners and one, Persia, became much stronger than the other. Chapter 8 pictures the same empire as a ram with two horns, one higher than the other (8:3, 20). The three ribs in its mouth may represent the major conquests it had swallowed, though we cannot be sure which ones. Notice that it is told to devour. Even the beasts act only when permitted.

After this I looked, and behold, another, like a leopard, with four wings of a bird on its back. And the beast had four heads, and dominion was given to it.

The third beast matches the bronze: Greece. The leopard is fast, and with four wings it is faster still. That fits Alexander the Great, who conquered the whole Persian empire in about ten years. The four heads fit what happened after his early death, when his empire was divided among four of his generals. Chapter 8 describes exactly that: when the great horn was broken, four kingdoms shall arise from his nation, but not with his power (8:22).

Again, notice the words dominion was given to it. No empire takes power on its own. Every one of them receives it from the Most High, for as long as he allows.

verseByVerse.quote: After this I saw in the night visions, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet. It was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns. I considered the horns, and behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots. And behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this I saw in the night visions, and behold, a fourth beast, terrifying and dreadful and exceedingly strong. It had great iron teeth; it devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet. It was different from all the beasts that were before it, and it had ten horns.

The fourth beast is so terrible that Daniel cannot compare it to any known animal. Its iron teeth link it to the legs of iron in chapter 2. It does not only conquer. It crushes and tramples what is left. As explained at chapter 2, the traditional understanding, followed here, sees this as Rome, which crushed every power in its path. (Those who read the four kingdoms as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece see this beast as Greece.)

The beast has ten horns. In the Bible a horn is a symbol of strength, and especially of a king's power. The angel will explain that the ten horns are ten kings (v. 24).

I considered the horns, and behold, there came up among them another horn, a little one, before which three of the first horns were plucked up by the roots. And behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.

Daniel's attention fixes on a little horn that grows among the others and uproots three of them. It has eyes like the eyes of a man, suggesting intelligence and watchfulness, and a mouth speaking great things, boastful words against God (v. 25). This small horn becomes the focus of the rest of the vision.

Who is this little horn? Christians have held three main views. Many believe it is a final ruler who will oppose God and persecute his people at the end of history, the one Paul calls the man of lawlessness who exalts himself against every so-called god or object of worship (2 Thess 2:3-4), and whom Revelation pictures as a beast with a mouth uttering haughty and blasphemous words (Rev 13:5). Others, who take the fourth kingdom as Greece, identify the little horn with Antiochus IV, a Greek king who persecuted the Jews in the second century BC (and chapter 8 does describe him). Many Protestants in the centuries after the Reformation saw the horn as the papacy. The first view is the one most widely held today among Reformed and other evangelical interpreters. It also fits the chapter's own claim that the horn's defeat is followed directly by the final judgment and the everlasting kingdom (vv. 26-27). John adds a helpful balance: as you have heard that antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have come (1 John 2:18). The final enemy will be foreshadowed by many proud rulers before him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–14 — The Ancient of Days and the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Thrones are placed and the Ancient of Days took his seat, dazzling white and surrounded by fire and countless servants; the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened (vv. 9-10). The beast is destroyed and the others lose their dominion (vv. 11-12). Then with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, who receives from the Ancient of Days an everlasting dominion over all peoples (vv. 13-14).
verseByVerse.theology: God sits in judgment over the beasts and gives the everlasting kingdom to the Son of Man, Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As I looked, thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames; its wheels were burning fire. A stream of fire issued and came out from before him; a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As I looked, thrones were placed, and the Ancient of Days took his seat; his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames; its wheels were burning fire.

Suddenly the scene moves from the stormy sea to heaven's courtroom. While the little horn is still boasting on earth, thrones were placed in heaven, and a judge takes his seat.

He is called the Ancient of Days, a title found only in this chapter. It means the one who is old beyond all time, the eternal God. The beasts are new arrivals in history, rising and falling. He was there before them all. His white clothing speaks of purity and his white hair of wisdom and eternal age. His throne is fiery flames, with wheels of fire, like the living throne-chariot Ezekiel saw by the Chebar canal (Ezek 1). Fire speaks of holiness and judgment. This throne is not fixed in one place. It moves wherever God wills.

Then, in the New Testament, something astonishing happens. When John sees the risen Jesus, he describes him with the words of this verse: The hairs of his head were white, like white wool, like snow (Rev 1:14). The features of the Ancient of Days belong to Christ. He shares the eternal glory of God.

A stream of fire issued and came out from before him; a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him; the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened.

A river of fire flows from the throne, and countless heavenly servants surround it, ten thousand times ten thousand, more than can be counted. Then comes the solemn moment: the court sat in judgment, and the books were opened. The books are the records of what the beasts have done. Nothing has been forgotten. Revelation uses the same picture: books were opened... And the dead were judged by what was written in the books, according to what they had done (Rev 20:12).

This is deeply comforting for God's persecuted people. Tyrants may seem to act without consequences. But every word, every cruelty and every martyr is recorded, and the court will sit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I looked then because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking. And as I looked, the beast was killed, and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire. As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I looked then because of the sound of the great words that the horn was speaking. And as I looked, the beast was killed, and its body destroyed and given over to be burned with fire.

Daniel's eyes are drawn back to earth by the noise of the horn's boasting. It is still talking. And then, with no battle described, the verdict is carried out. The beast was killed. All its loud words cannot save it. He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision (Ps 2:4).

As for the rest of the beasts, their dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged for a season and a time.

The earlier beasts are treated differently. Their power to rule is taken away, but they are not destroyed at once. This probably reflects the way history works. When one empire conquered another, the conquered peoples and their cultures did not disappear. Babylon's people lived on under Persia, and Persia's under Greece. Each empire lost its rule but survived for a while inside the next. The fourth beast, however, will be completely destroyed at the final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: "I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him.

This is the high point of the chapter and one of the most important verses in the Bible.

After four beasts comes one like a son of man, which means one who looks like a human being. The contrast is intentional. The kingdoms of the world are beastly. God's kingdom will be ruled by one who is truly human, as God intended humanity to rule from the beginning (Gen 1:26-28).

But he is more than a man. He comes with the clouds of heaven. In the Old Testament, riding on the clouds is a picture used of God himself: he makes the clouds his chariot (Ps 104:3). This figure is human, yet he travels as God travels. And he is brought into the very presence of the Ancient of Days.

Jesus called himself the Son of Man more than any other title, and he took it from this verse. At his trial, when the high priest demanded, Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?, Jesus answered: I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven (Mark 14:61-62). The high priest tore his clothes and charged him with blasphemy. He understood exactly what Jesus was claiming: to be the divine-human King of Daniel 7.

Notice the direction of travel. The son of man comes to the Ancient of Days, from earth to heaven's throne. Many interpreters see this fulfilled first in Christ's ascension, when a cloud took him out of their sight (Acts 1:9) and he was enthroned in heaven. Stephen, as he was dying, saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:56). And the same Jesus will come again with the clouds to earth: Behold, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him (Rev 1:7). His kingdom has been received, and it will be revealed.

And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed.

Everything the beasts grasped at is now given to him: dominion and glory and a kingdom. Nebuchadnezzar demanded that peoples, nations, and languages bow to his image (3:4). Now all peoples, nations, and languages will serve the Son of Man. And his kingdom, unlike every beastly empire, shall not pass away.

After his resurrection, Jesus spoke as the one who had received this kingdom: All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me (Matt 28:18). That is why the church goes to all nations with the gospel. The kingdom of the Son of Man is gathering its people from every language on earth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–22 — The Saints Shall Receive the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Troubled, Daniel asks one of those standing there for the meaning (vv. 15-16). These four great beasts are four kings who shall arise out of the earth. But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever (vv. 17-18). Daniel asks especially about the fourth beast and the horn that made war with the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came and the saints possessed the kingdom (vv. 19-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The people of God may be overpowered for a time, but the kingdom is finally theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: "As for me, Daniel, my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me. I approached one of those who stood there and asked him the truth concerning all this. So he told me and made known to me the interpretation of the things. 'These four great beasts are four kings who shall arise out of the earth. But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever, forever and ever.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As for me, Daniel, my spirit within me was anxious, and the visions of my head alarmed me.

Daniel was deeply disturbed. The ESV notes that within me is literally "within its sheath", a picture of the body as the sheath that holds the spirit, like a sword. The vision shook him to the core. Seeing the future clearly did not make Daniel proud or excited. It made him tremble. Prophecy is not given to satisfy curiosity but to prepare God's people.

I approached one of those who stood there and asked him the truth concerning all this. So he told me and made known to me the interpretation of the things.

Daniel does what every reader of prophecy should do. He asks for the true meaning, and he receives it from heaven. We too need God's own interpretation, and we have it, in the rest of Scripture.

'These four great beasts are four kings who shall arise out of the earth.

The beasts came up from the sea (v. 3). Here they arise out of the earth. Both images make the same point: these kingdoms have a purely earthly origin, in contrast to the son of man who comes with the clouds of heaven. The kings stand for their kingdoms (v. 23).

But the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom and possess the kingdom forever, forever and ever.'

This is the heart of the explanation, given in one sentence. After all the beasts, the saints of the Most High shall receive the kingdom. The saints are God's holy people, those set apart to belong to him. The kingdom given to the son of man in verse 14 is also given to his people. The King shares his reign with those who belong to him.

Some readers have taken this to mean that the son of man is simply a symbol for the saints. But the New Testament shows how the two belong together. Jesus is the King, and his people reign with him. The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne (Rev 3:21). If we endure, we will also reign with him (2 Tim 2:12). And Jesus told his small, weak band of followers: Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father's good pleasure to give you the kingdom (Luke 12:32).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast, which was different from all the rest, exceedingly terrifying, with its teeth of iron and claws of bronze, and which devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet, and about the ten horns that were on its head, and the other horn that came up and before which three of them fell, the horn that had eyes and a mouth that spoke great things, and that seemed greater than its companions. As I looked, this horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them, until the Ancient of Days came, and judgment was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then I desired to know the truth about the fourth beast, which was different from all the rest, exceedingly terrifying, with its teeth of iron and claws of bronze, and which devoured and broke in pieces and stamped what was left with its feet,

and about the ten horns that were on its head, and the other horn that came up and before which three of them fell, the horn that had eyes and a mouth that spoke great things, and that seemed greater than its companions.

Daniel is most troubled by the fourth beast and its little horn, just as we would expect. He adds new details: the beast also had claws of bronze, and the little horn seemed greater than its companions. It started small, but it grew until it overshadowed all the others.

As I looked, this horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them,

Here is something the first description did not mention. The horn made war with the saints and prevailed over them. God's people will not always win in this world. For a time they will be defeated, persecuted and killed. Revelation says the same of the beast: it was allowed to make war on the saints and to conquer them (Rev 13:7). Christians should not be shocked when faithfulness leads to suffering. It was foretold.

until the Ancient of Days came, and judgment was given for the saints of the Most High, and the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom.

But the key word is until. The horn's victory has an end date. Until the Ancient of Days came. Then judgment was given for the saints. The court rules in favor of the persecuted. The kingdom that the horn tried to seize is handed to the people it oppressed. Paul reminds believers of their future: do you not know that the saints will judge the world? (1 Cor 6:2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–28 — Time, Times, and Half a Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fourth kingdom will devour the whole earth; from it come ten kings and another who puts down three (vv. 23-24). He will speak against the Most High, wear out the saints and try to change times and law, for a time, times, and half a time (v. 25). Then the court will sit, his dominion will be destroyed, and the kingdom will be given to the people of the saints (vv. 26-27). Daniel is alarmed and keeps the matter in his heart (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The persecution of God's people is real but limited, and God's judgment and kingdom are certain.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus he said: 'As for the fourth beast, there shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be different from all the kingdoms, and it shall devour the whole earth, and trample it down, and break it to pieces. As for the ten horns, out of this kingdom ten kings shall arise, and another shall arise after them; he shall be different from the former ones, and shall put down three kings. He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High, and shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand for a time, times, and half a time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus he said: 'As for the fourth beast, there shall be a fourth kingdom on earth, which shall be different from all the kingdoms, and it shall devour the whole earth, and trample it down, and break it to pieces.

As for the ten horns, out of this kingdom ten kings shall arise, and another shall arise after them; he shall be different from the former ones, and shall put down three kings.

The angel explains the fourth beast. It is a kingdom that swallows the whole earth. From it come ten kings, and then one more, who is different and overthrows three of them. Some take the ten as literal rulers of a final world order. Others take ten as a round number for the full set of powers that come from the fourth kingdom. Revelation also speaks of ten horns as ten kings who have not yet received royal power, ruling together with the beast (Rev 17:12).

He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High, and shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand for a time, times, and half a time.

Here are the marks of this final enemy of God. He will speak words against the Most High, exalting himself against God. He will wear out the saints, not always by a single violent blow, but by constant, grinding pressure. And he will think to change the times and the law, trying to overturn God's order: the sacred calendar, the worship of God and the moral law itself. Every age has seen rulers who tried to redefine what is good, erase the memory of God from public life and wear down believers until they give up.

But notice that his power is given. They shall be given into his hand, for a set period. A time, times, and half a time most likely means one year, two years and half a year: three and a half. Revelation uses the same expression (Rev 12:14) and its equivalents, forty-two months and 1,260 days (Rev 11:2-3). Some Christians, especially dispensationalists, take this as a literal period of three and a half years at the very end of history. Many others, including many in the Reformed tradition, take it as a symbolic number for a limited period of persecution. Three and a half is half of seven, the number of completeness. The enemy's time is broken off halfway. Either way, the comfort is the same. The persecution is real, but it is measured, limited and controlled by God.

verseByVerse.quote: But the court shall sit in judgment, and his dominion shall be taken away, to be consumed and destroyed to the end. And the kingdom and the dominion and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High; his kingdom shall be an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.' "Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts greatly alarmed me, and my color changed, but I kept the matter in my heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the court shall sit in judgment, and his dominion shall be taken away, to be consumed and destroyed to the end.

The angel ends where the vision did, with the court. But the court shall sit. However loud the horn becomes, however long the saints are worn down, a day of judgment is coming, and his dominion will be destroyed to the end. He will never rise again.

And the kingdom and the dominion and the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High; his kingdom shall be an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey him.'

All the greatness of the kingdoms under the whole heaven, everything the beasts ever possessed, will be given to God's people. The ESV notes that the second half of the verse could also be read "their kingdom shall be an everlasting kingdom, and all dominions shall serve and obey them". Both readings are true together. The kingdom belongs to God and his King, and he shares it with his people. And they will reign forever and ever (Rev 22:5).

"Here is the end of the matter. As for me, Daniel, my thoughts greatly alarmed me, and my color changed, but I kept the matter in my heart."

Daniel does not come away from the vision with a chart of dates. He comes away shaken, pale and thoughtful. And he kept the matter in my heart, treasuring it and pondering it, as Mary would do with the words spoken about her Son: Mary treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart (Luke 2:19).

That is the right response to biblical prophecy. Its purpose is not to feed speculation about which world leader is the little horn. Its purpose is to steady God's people. The beasts are real, and they may prevail for a while. But the court is already seated, the Son of Man has already received the kingdom, and the saints will possess it forever. When the news seems full of beasts, Christians can lift their eyes to the throne.

7.title: One Like a Son of Man
7.overview:
In the first year of Belshazzar, Daniel has a dream and writes it down. He sees the four winds stirring up the great sea and four great beasts coming out of it: a lion with eagles' wings, whose wings are plucked off and which is made to stand like a man and given a man's mind; a bear raised up on one side with three ribs in its mouth, told to devour much flesh; and a leopard with four wings and four heads, given dominion. A fourth beast, terrifying and exceedingly strong, with great iron teeth, devours and tramples everything, and it has ten horns. A little horn with eyes like a man and a boastful mouth comes up among them, uprooting three (vv. 1-8).

Thrones are placed, and the Ancient of Days takes his seat, his clothing white as snow and his hair like pure wool, his throne fiery flames. Thousands upon thousands serve him; the court sits in judgment and the books are opened. The beast is killed and burned, and the other beasts lose their dominion. Then one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given everlasting dominion, glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations and languages should serve him (vv. 9-14).

Daniel, alarmed, asks one who stands there for the meaning. The four beasts are four kings, but the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom forever. Daniel asks about the fourth beast and the horn that made war with the saints and prevailed until the Ancient of Days came and judgment was given for the saints (vv. 15-22).

The fourth beast is a fourth kingdom that will devour the whole earth. Ten kings will arise from it, and another who will put down three. He will speak against the Most High, wear out the saints and seek to change the times and the law, and they will be given into his hand for a time, times and half a time. But the court will sit, his dominion will be destroyed, and the kingdom will be given to the people of the saints of the Most High. Daniel is greatly alarmed and keeps the matter in his heart (vv. 23-28).
7.theology:
God rules over the turmoil of history; the empires of the world, however glorious they appear, are beastly in God's sight and hold power only as it is given to them (vv. 2-7).

The Ancient of Days is the eternal Judge who records every deed; the court will sit and the proud will be destroyed (vv. 9-12, 26; Ps 2:4; Rev 20:12).

The one like a son of man, coming with the clouds and receiving an everlasting kingdom, is Jesus Christ, who shares the glory of God, has received all authority and will come again (vv. 13-14; Mark 14:61-62; Acts 1:9; 7:56; Matt 28:18; Rev 1:7, 13-14).

The saints share the kingdom of their King and will reign with him forever (vv. 18, 22, 27; Luke 12:32; Rev 3:21; 22:5; 2 Tim 2:12; 1 Cor 6:2).

A final enemy will blaspheme God and persecute his people, foreshadowed by many antichrists, but his time is limited and his defeat certain (vv. 8, 21, 24-26; 2 Thess 2:3-4; 1 John 2:18; Rev 13:5-7).

Prophecy is given not to feed speculation but to steady God's people in suffering (vv. 15, 28).
7.examples:
A storm-tossed sea with monsters rising from it.

A lion that loses its wings and learns to stand like a man.

A small horn with a very large mouth.

A courtroom where the books are opened.

A human figure riding the clouds to the throne of God.

A high priest tearing his robes at Jesus' answer.

Saints worn down, until the Ancient of Days comes.

A prophet who ends his vision pale, silent and pondering.
